tracks.legalName: Petition for Retroactive First Offender Treatment, Exoneration and Discharge under O.C.G.A. § 42-8-66
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: An individual who qualified for first offender sentencing but was not informed of that eligibility, or who was sentenced between March 18, 1968 and October 31, 1982 to incarceration not exceeding one year and would otherwise have qualified, may petition the court in which they were convicted for retroactive first offender treatment. The petition may be filed only with the consent of the prosecuting attorney, obtained before filing. A hearing is held if requested by the petitioner or the prosecuting attorney or if the court desires one. The court may grant if it finds by a preponderance that the defendant was eligible at the time of the original sentencing, or qualifies under the 1968 to 1982 provision, and that the ends of justice and the welfare of society are served. There is no filing fee. On a grant the conviction becomes a first offender discharge, which is not a conviction, and the court sends the order to the petitioner, the prosecuting attorney, the Georgia Crime Information Center and the Department of Driver Services, both of which must modify their records.

tracks.legalName: Conviction Expungement, first-time drug offender, HRS § 706-622.5(4)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Two stages, both settled. Stage one is a written motion in the participant's own existing penal case, filed in the court that sentenced or convicted them, seeking a court order expunging the record of conviction; stage two is the HCJDC 159(b) Expungement Application submitted to the Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center with a copy of that order attached. The stage-one vehicle is fixed by Haw. R. Penal P. 47(a), which provides that "An application to the court for an order shall be by motion", so Hawaii penal practice does not distinguish an application from a motion however the statute words it; the Rules of Penal Procedure govern because Rule 54(a) applies them to all penal proceedings and none of these provisions supplies its own procedure. Mandatory. 'the court shall issue a court order to expunge'. The proviso states conditions, not a discretion. The court has no listed ground to refuse a qualifying application. No official statewide Hawaii Judiciary expungement form exists for stage one in any circuit, so a controlled custom pleading is permitted and is the only available strategy. Venue follows the offence and is a participant input rather than a track constant. Nothing here makes the Hawaii implementation ready.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of a Kansas Municipal Court Conviction or Diversion under K.S.A. 12-4516
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person convicted of a violation of a city ordinance may petition the convicting municipal court to expunge the conviction and related arrest records once three or more years have elapsed since satisfying the sentence imposed or discharge from probation, parole or a suspended sentence; a person who has fulfilled the terms of a diversion agreement based on a city ordinance violation may petition once three or more years have elapsed since those terms were fulfilled. Longer five-year and ten-year periods apply to the offences listed in (d) and to DUI-equivalent ordinance violations under (e), and a one-year period applies under (c) to a prostitution-equivalent ordinance violation where the petitioner can prove coercion. The court sets a hearing and causes notice to be given to the prosecuting attorney and the arresting law enforcement agency, and shall order expungement on three findings: no felony conviction in the past two years with no such proceeding pending or being instituted, that the petitioner's circumstances and behaviour warrant expungement, and that expungement is consistent with the public welfare. There is no firearms finding, because a municipal ordinance conviction is not a felony.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of a City Ordinance Arrest Record under K.S.A. 12-4516a
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Any person who has been arrested on a violation of a city ordinance may petition the court to expunge the arrest record. When the petition is filed the court sets a hearing date and causes notice to be given to the prosecuting attorney and the arresting law enforcement agency, and the official court file is separated from other court records and disclosed only to a judge, designated court staff, the prosecuting attorney, the arresting agency or others by court order. A municipal court may prescribe a fee as costs, except that no fee may be charged to a person arrested as a result of being a victim of identity theft. At the hearing the court shall order the arrest record and subsequent court proceedings expunged on finding mistaken identity; that a court found no probable cause for the arrest; that the petitioner was found not guilty; that the arrest was for a violation of an ordinance prohibited by K.S.A. 12-16,134(a) or (b) adopted before July 1, 2014; or that expungement would be in the best interests of justice and charges have been dismissed or no charges have been or are likely to be filed.

authority: State v. Anderson, 12 Kan. App. 2d 342, 744 P.2d 143 (1987)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person convicted in Kansas of a traffic infraction, cigarette or tobacco infraction, misdemeanour, class D or E felony, nongrid felony, nondrug grid severity level 6 through 10 felony, drug grid severity level 4 felony for crimes committed between July 1, 1993 and June 30, 2012, or drug grid severity level 5 felony for crimes committed on or after July 1, 2012, may petition the convicting court to expunge the conviction and related arrest records once the applicable period has elapsed since satisfying the sentence imposed or being discharged from probation, a community correctional services programme, parole, postrelease supervision, conditional release or a suspended sentence. Longer periods apply under (c) and (d). At the hearing the court shall order expungement if it makes the four findings in (h). The clock runs from sentence satisfaction or discharge from supervision — not from arrest and not from conviction.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of a Kansas Arrest Record under K.S.A. 22-2410
authority: State v. Yrigolla, 38 Kan. App. 2d 1029, 175 P.3d 276 (2008)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Any person who has been arrested in Kansas may petition the district court to expunge the arrest record. There is no waiting period. On filing, the court sets a hearing date and causes notice to be given to the prosecuting attorney and the arresting law enforcement agency, and the official court file is separated from other court records and disclosed only to a judge, designated court staff, the prosecuting attorney, the arresting agency or others by court order. At the hearing the court shall order the arrest record and subsequent court proceedings expunged on finding that the arrest occurred because of mistaken identity, that a court found there was no probable cause for the arrest, that the petitioner was found not guilty, or that expungement would be in the best interests of justice and charges have been dismissed or no charges have been or are likely to be filed. This is the correct route for an arrest-only record: K.S.A. 21-6614 expunges a conviction or a diversion and related arrest records, so with neither there is nothing for it to attach to.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Relief from Drug Offender Registration under K.S.A. 22-4908, Combined with Expungement under K.S.A. 21-6614
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: K.S.A. 21-6614(f) bars expungement of any conviction or any part of the criminal record of a person required to register under the Kansas Offender Registration Act while registration is required, except as provided in K.S.A. 22-4908. Under that section a drug offender who has registered for at least five years after the date of parole, discharge or release, or five years from the date of conviction if not confined, may file a verified petition for relief from registration in the district court of the county of conviction. The Judicial Council has developed the petition form the statute requires. On relief the court orders removal from the registry and notifies the KBI within 14 days. Subsection (i) permits the offender to combine the petition for relief with a petition for expungement under K.S.A. 21-6614 where the offence requiring registration is otherwise eligible for expungement. Sex offenders and violent offenders are not authorised to seek relief.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Expungement of Acquittals and Dismissals With Prejudice (KRS 431.076(1)(a))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person is acquitted, or an order dismisses with prejudice all criminal charges in a case and the dismissal was not in exchange for a guilty plea to another charge, the court enters an order of automatic expungement thirty days after the judgment becomes final. The statute states that the order shall not require any action by the person. All criminal records in the custody of the court and of any other agency, including law enforcement records, are expunged and the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred. KRS 431.076(8) makes the section retroactive except for subsection (1)(a), so the automatic route does not reach dispositions before 15 July 2020.
officialFormRefs: KRS 431.076, Expungement of records of acquittal or dismissal
Kentucky Circuit Court Clerks' Manual, July 2026

scopedOutStatements.text: The automatic subsection does not reach dispositions before 15 July 2020. KRS 431.076(8) makes the rest of the section retroactive but excepts subsection (1)(a).

tracks.legalName: Segregation of Arrest Records After Acquittal, Dismissal or Withdrawal of Charges (KRS 17.142)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A law enforcement or other public agency holding arrest records, fingerprints, photographs or other data must, on the written request of the arrestee, segregate those records into a file separate from those of convicted persons where the person was found innocent or all charges relating to the offence were dismissed or withdrawn. The person may instead apply to the court, which shall forthwith issue an order to all law enforcement agencies. Each agency must notify every agency it shared the records with, and the segregated record must show the disposition. Records subject to KRS 431.076 or KRS 431.078 are sealed under those statutes instead.
officialFormRefs: Kentucky Circuit Court Clerks' Manual, July 2026

scopedOutStatements.text: Records that are eligible under KRS 431.076 or KRS 431.078, which should be expunged rather than segregated because expungement is materially stronger.
Route to KRS 431.076 or KRS 431.078 first. KRS 17.142(4) sends records subject to those statutes there instead, which leaves withdrawn charges as the clearest residual use of this route.

tracks.legalName: Routing of a Pretrial Diversion Disposition (KRS 533.258)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: On successful completion of pretrial diversion the charges are listed as dismissed-diverted and do not constitute a criminal conviction. The person need not disclose the disposition on an application for employment, licensure or otherwise unless federal law requires it, and diversion records may not be introduced as evidence without the defendant's consent. The designation is not expungement: the record still exists until it is expunged, so this node reads the disposition and routes to the automatic or petition track.
officialFormRefs: KRS 533.258, Effect of successful completion of pretrial diversion
Kentucky Circuit Court Clerks' Manual, July 2026

tracks.legalName: Expungement Certification Request to the Administrative Office of the Courts (KRS 431.079)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Every petition or application seeking expungement of a conviction must include a certification of eligibility issued by the Administrative Office of the Courts. The participant requests it on the AOC Records Unit form, pays the statutory fee, and the AOC produces the certification after a Kentucky State Police records check. The certification is an evidentiary attachment: it decides nothing, and an adverse certification does not stop the clerk from accepting a petition.

tracks.legalName: Application to Vacate and Expunge a Felony Conviction After a Full Pardon (KRS 431.073(1)(c))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where the Governor has granted a full pardon, the pardoned conviction is eligible for vacatur and expungement on the same verified application as any other KRS 431.073 case. The Class D limitation and the enumerated-offence list do not apply on this branch: the pardon itself is the eligibility ground. The five-year wait in KRS 431.073(2)(a) is not branch-specific and still applies.

tracks.legalName: Application to Vacate and Expunge a Class D Felony Conviction (KRS 431.073)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: On a verified application filed in the original criminal case, the court may vacate an eligible Class D felony conviction, dismiss the charges with prejudice and order the record expunged. Relief is discretionary. The record is expunged only on full payment of the $250 expungement fee, which may be paid in instalments under KRS 534.020. Vacatur does not revive an expired limitations period, is not a finding of legal error or innocence, and does not nullify findings of fact or law.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Vacate and Expunge a Juvenile Record (KRS 610.330)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: On petition, the court vacates the adjudication and expunges all records in the custody of the court and of any other agency, including law enforcement records and public and private elementary and secondary school records. The proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and all index references are deleted. Relief covers status offences and public offences that would be felonies, misdemeanors or violations if committed by an adult, adjudicated under KRS Chapters 630, 635 or 645. There is a separate automatic branch under KRS 610.330(7) where a petition is dismissed or the child is found not delinquent, which requires no action by the child.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of a Misdemeanor, Violation or Traffic Infraction Conviction (KRS 431.078)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: On petition, the court expunges a misdemeanor, violation or traffic infraction conviction, together with any misdemeanor, violation or traffic charges dismissed or amended in the same criminal action, five years after the later of sentence completion or successful completion of probation. Relief is mandatory for a single offence or a series arising from a single incident and discretionary for a series that did not. Once expunged the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and the participant need not disclose them.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of an Acquittal, Dismissal or Failure to Indict (KRS 431.076)

tracks.legalName: Motion to Void a First Controlled-Substance Possession Conviction and Seal the Records (KRS 218A.275)

tracks.legalName: Motion to Expunge Record of Arrest That Did Not Result in a Conviction (La. C.Cr.P. art. 976)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Article 976(A) lets a person move to expunge a record of arrest for a felony or misdemeanour that did not result in conviction where the person was not prosecuted and the time limitation has expired, the district attorney declined to prosecute every offence arising out of the arrest including because a pretrial diversion programme was completed, the proceedings were finally disposed of by dismissal, sustaining of a motion to quash or acquittal, or the person was judicially determined to be factually innocent and entitled to compensation under R.S. 15:572.8. Article 976(B) bars expungement of an arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated, or a parish or municipal equivalent, where the person was placed in a pretrial diversion programme, until five years have elapsed since the date of arrest. Article 975 bars filing by a person in the physical custody of the Department of Public Safety and Corrections serving a sentence at hard labour. Relief is effectively mandatory: under Article 980 the court grants where no timely objection is filed and the mover is legally entitled.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Expunge a Record of Arrest and Conviction of a Misdemeanor Offense (La. C.Cr.P. art. 977)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Article 977(A) lets a person move to expunge a record of arrest and conviction of a misdemeanour on either of two grounds. Under (A)(1) the conviction was set aside and the prosecution dismissed under Article 894(B), which is the separate Article 987 mechanism. Under (A)(2) more than five years have elapsed since the person completed any sentence, deferred adjudication, or period of probation or parole, the person has not been convicted of any felony offence during that five-year period and has no felony charge pending; the motion must include a certification obtained from the district attorney verifying, to his knowledge, no felony convictions during the five-year period and no pending felony charges under a bill of information or indictment. Article 977(C) bars expungement where the misdemeanour conviction arose from circumstances involving or resulting from an arrest for a sex offence as defined in R.S. 15:541 — expressly preserving interim expungement under Article 985.1 — and where the conviction was for domestic abuse battery or for stalking under R.S. 14:40.2. Confirmed against the current official text, whose source notes run through Acts 2023, No. 342.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Expunge Record of Arrest and Conviction of a Felony Offense (La. C.Cr.P. art. 978)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Article 978(A) lets a person move to expunge a record of arrest and conviction of a felony where the conviction was set aside and the prosecution dismissed under Article 893(E); or where more than ten years have elapsed since the person completed any sentence, deferred adjudication, or period of probation or parole, the person has not been convicted of any other criminal offence during that ten-year period and has no criminal charge pending, with a district attorney certification; or where the person is entitled to a first offender pardon for the offence, provided it is not a crime of violence or a sex offence. Article 978(B) bars expungement, and bars filing, where the person was convicted of the commission or attempted commission of a crime of violence under R.S. 14:2(B) unless Paragraph E applies; a sex offence or a criminal offence against a victim who is a minor under R.S. 15:541, with a narrow carnal-knowledge exception; a violation of the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law, except five listed categories that may be expunged; or domestic abuse battery. Article 978(E) permits the court, after a contradictory hearing, to order expungement for aggravated battery, second degree battery, aggravated criminal damage to property, simple robbery, purse snatching, or illegal use of weapons or dangerous instrumentalities on the ten-year clean-period conditions. tracks.legalName: Interim Motion to Expunge a Felony Arrest from Criminal History (La. C.Cr.P. art. 985.1)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Article 985.1(A) permits an interim motion to expunge a felony arrest from the criminal history of a person who was convicted of a misdemeanour offence arising out of that original felony arrest; only the original felony arrest is expunged. Article 985.1(B) makes the interim motion separate and distinct from expungement of a final conviction under Articles 976, 977 and 978. Article 985.1(C) applies the Article 979 et seq. procedures and fees except as provided in (D), and Article 985.1(D) provides that the motion is not subject to the time limitations of Article 977(A)(2) or 978(A)(2) and permits more than one interim expungement. Article 977(C)(1) expressly preserves interim expungement even where the misdemeanour conviction itself is barred by the sex-offence exclusion. Article 986 makes Article 994 the motion form and Article 995 the order form. Confirmed against the current official text; Article 985.1 has not been amended since Acts 2014, No. 145.

tracks.legalName: Automated Expungement of Qualifying Records (La. C.Cr.P. art. 985.2)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Article 985.2(A) directs the Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information to identify within its criminal repository database all records with a Case Management Information System number and final dispositions for individuals eligible for expungement under Articles 976, 977 and 978. Article 985.2(B) provides that beginning 1 January 2025 a defendant may submit a request through the Bureau for expungement through the automated process, the request containing the defendant's name, date of birth, last four digits of the Social Security number, arrest date and case number, and requires the Bureau to expunge any eligible records within thirty days of receipt and send them to the Louisiana Supreme Court Case Management Information System. Paragraphs (C) and (D) govern clerk verification and notice to the district attorney, sheriff and arresting agency. Article 985.2(G) provides that the Article shall be subject to the appropriate funding necessary for implementation and provided for in the executive budget for Fiscal Year 2025-2026. The current official text at legis.la.gov carries the operative note 'Article 985.2 eff. upon appropriation of monies by the Legislature. See Acts 2023, No. 454.' tracks.legalName: Immediate Expungement; Judicial Discretion (La. C.Cr.P. art. 985.3)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Article 985.3(A) provides that the court MAY ORDER the immediate expungement of the record of the arrest and conviction of the violation that necessitated participation in the probation or programme, by a person who is otherwise eligible for an expungement, upon the successful completion of a court-ordered probation or alternative sentencing programme. Article 985.3(B) provides that ONLY THE FORM PROVIDED IN ARTICLE 992 shall be used to expunge the record of such a person. Article 985.3(C) provides that the immediate expungement shall be served pursuant to Article 982 and shall include the court record with the signed order together with the bill of information, the sentencing minutes, and any documents or records relevant to the arrest incident and plea agreements, if available. The Article was enacted by Acts 2024, No. 560 (2024 H.B. 416), whose digest describes it as providing for a court-ordered automatic expungement in certain cases. The full text was obtained and read for this normalization; the review had identified the Article but not read it.

tracks.legalName: Deferred Disposition — Outcome Classification and Sealing-Eligibility Routing (17-A M.R.S. ch. 67, subch. 4; 15 M.R.S. § 2262(3))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A deferred disposition is not a record-clearing mechanism and produces no relief of its own. It is a disposition status with two possible outcomes and one sharp cross-track consequence, and it is modelled as a routing node for exactly that reason. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1901 a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State; under § 1903, on compliance and the State's motion, the court permits withdrawal of the plea and the State dismisses the charging instrument with prejudice. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. Where the case instead ends in conviction of a reduced offence, that conviction is evaluated on its own terms under chapter 310-A and qualifies only if it lands inside the § 2261(6) eligible set. The cross-track consequence is the one that matters most: under 15 M.R.S. § 2262(3) a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition, since the person fully satisfied the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction, is an absolute disqualifier for the general sealing track. A deferred disposition is therefore good news for the case it resolves and bad news for a prior conviction the participant wanted sealed.

Confidential information may be disseminated only to the recipients listed in § 705, and a criminal justice agency may not confirm its existence or nonexistence to anyone not entitled to receive it. tracks.legalName: Business Screening Service Dispute for Correction or Deletion of Criminal History Record Information (10 M.R.S. c. 239, § 1500-CC)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Chapter 239 regulates how a business screening service handles Maine criminal history record information. A business screening service under § 1500-AA is a person regularly engaged in the business of collecting, assembling, evaluating or disseminating criminal history record information about specific individuals for a fee, excluding a government entity and the news media. Under § 1500-CC, where the completeness or accuracy of a record is disputed by its subject, the service shall investigate WITHOUT CHARGE; must review and consider all relevant information the subject submits and determine whether its record accurately reflects the official record maintained by the State Bureau of Identification; must correct a record that does not accurately reflect the official record; and — the operative remedy here — if the disputed record is found to be sealed or the subject of a pardon, SHALL PROMPTLY DELETE the record. The service may terminate an investigation it reasonably determines is frivolous, but must then state the specific reasons and describe the information it needs. Within thirty days of receiving notice of the dispute the service must notify the subject of the results, including whether the investigation was completed or terminated and what records were corrected or deleted. tracks.legalName: Motion to Seal Criminal History Record Information (15 M.R.S. ch. 310-A, §§ 2262-2264)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Chapter 310-A permits a person to move, in the underlying criminal proceeding, to seal the criminal history record information relating to one specific eligible criminal conviction. Under § 2262 the conviction must be an eligible criminal conviction; at least four years must have passed since the person fully satisfied each of the sentencing alternatives imposed under 17-A M.R.S. § 1502(2); the person must not have been convicted of another crime in Maine and must not have had a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition since satisfying the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction; must not have been convicted of a crime in another jurisdiction in that period; and must have no presently pending criminal charges in Maine or elsewhere. Former § 2262(6), an age condition, was repealed by PL 2023, c. 666, § 3. 'Eligible criminal conviction' under § 2261(6)(A) means a current or former Class E crime other than one under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 11, and under § 2261(6)(B) five specifically listed marijuana offences committed before 30 January 2017. Relief is mandatory once proven: § 2264(5) directs that the court shall grant the motion where the person establishes each prerequisite by a preponderance of the evidence. authority: City of St. Paul v. Froysland, 246 N.W.2d 435 (Minn. 1976)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A judicially recognised inherent authority to seal judicial branch records, outside chapter 609A. Ambaye sets two grounds: where the petitioner's constitutional rights may be seriously infringed by retention of the records, or, where constitutional rights are not involved, whether expungement yields a benefit to the petitioner commensurate with the disadvantages to the public and the burden on the court. tracks.legalName: Application for Expungement of a First Minor-in-Possession Violation (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 311.326)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 311.326 was read in full from the Revisor's current text, effective 28 August 2009, and it is a single unnumbered paragraph that does a great deal of work. After a period of not less than one year after reaching the age of twenty-one, a person who has pleaded guilty to or been found guilty of violating § 311.325 for the first time, and who since that conviction has not been convicted of any other alcohol-related offense, may apply to the court in which he or she was sentenced for an order expunging all official records of the arrest, plea, trial and conviction. No records shall be expunged if the person is licensed as a commercial motor vehicle driver or was operating a commercial motor vehicle as defined in § 302.700 at the time of the violation. If the court determines, upon review, that the person has not been convicted of any other alcohol-related offense at the time of the application and has had no other alcohol-related enforcement contacts as defined in § 302.525, the court shall enter an order of expungement. The effect is to restore the person to the status occupied before the arrest, plea or conviction as if the event had never happened, with a perjury shield. A person is entitled to only one expungement under the section, and courts and other state officials may keep records necessary to enforce that limit. tracks.legalName: Controlled-Substance Conditional Discharge and Expungement (Miss. Code Ann. § 41-29-150)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 41-29-150 carries Mississippi's controlled-substance conditional discharge and its associated expungement. A first-time eligible drug possession or paraphernalia case may be handled WITHOUT entering a judgment of guilt: the court defers proceedings, places the person on probation, and on successful completion discharges the person and dismisses the proceedings without an adjudication of guilt. Expungement of the record is then available on application to the court. The benefit is once-only, and a nonpublic record is retained for future eligibility checks, which is the same design as the § 99-19-71(3) first-offender retention. Trafficking under § 41-29-139 is a separate offence and is outside this route entirely; it is also independently excluded from felony expungement under § 99-19-71(2)(a)(iii). The complete current text was obtained on this pass, from the last enacted amendment, Laws 2010 ch. 460 § 2. The conditional discharge is § 41-29-150(d)(1) and the expungement remedy is § 41-29-150(d)(2). Eligibility reaches a person NOT previously convicted of violating § 41-29-139, or the laws of the United States or another state relating to narcotic drugs, stimulant or depressant substances, other controlled substances or marihuana, who is found guilty of a violation of § 41-29-139(c) or (d) — simple possession and paraphernalia — after trial or on a plea. tracks.legalName: First-Offense DUI Expungement (Miss. Code Ann. § 63-11-30)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 63-11-30 carries its own first-offence DUI expungement provision, entirely separate from the ordinary misdemeanour route, and a DUI must never be routed through § 99-19-71(1). Every condition must be met: at least five years after successful completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence; the person did not hold a commercial driver's licence or a commercial learner's permit at the time of the offence; the person did not refuse the blood or breath test; blood alcohol concentration below .16 where test results are available; no other DUI conviction and no pending DUI; the person has not previously had a DUI nonadjudication or a DUI expungement; and the person must justify the expungement to the court. Relief is discretionary. Venue is the CIRCUIT COURT of the county of conviction: the Attorney General has opined that a municipal court judge is not authorized to expunge a DUI conviction, although municipal and justice courts may handle expungement of nonadjudicated first-offence DUI charges in certain circumstances. That is the most likely way a Mississippi DUI petition gets filed in the wrong court. A third, fourth or subsequent DUI under § 63-11-30(2)(c) and (2)(d) is separately excluded from felony expungement under § 99-19-71(2)(a)(iv). tracks.legalName: First-Offender Misdemeanor Conviction Expungement (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(1))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 99-19-71(1), read from the enrolled text of 2026 HB 1546, provides: 'Any person who has been convicted of a misdemeanor that is not a traffic violation, and who is a first offender, may petition the justice, county, circuit or municipal court in which the conviction was had for an order to expunge any such conviction from all public records.' Subsection (1) contains NO waiting period, no completion requirement and no pending-charge restriction — the payment condition sits in subsection (2)(a) and is written for the felony track. Relief is permissive as to petitioning ('may petition') and the statute does not say the court shall grant, so it is treated as discretionary. Two elements carry the whole eligibility test: the offence must not be a traffic violation, and the person must be a first offender. tracks.legalName: Discretionary Expungement of Additional Justice Court or Municipal Court Misdemeanors (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 9-11-15(3), 21-23-7(6))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Two parallel provisions give the lower courts a discretionary power to expunge their own misdemeanour convictions: § 9-11-15(3) for justice court and § 21-23-7(6) for municipal court. They share one mechanism, one filing vehicle and one legal effect and differ only in which court is petitioned and which prosecutor is noticed, so they are modelled as ONE node with two venue branches rather than split. The complete text of both was obtained and compared word for word: every operative element is identical and the only differences are the court petitioned, the prosecutor noticed, clause order and pronoun style. Section 9-11-15(3) was added by Laws 2016 ch. 406 § 1 as a copy of the then-existing municipal provision; § 21-23-7(6) was last amended by Laws 2021 ch. 356. The court may, in its discretion, expunge the record of conviction of any or all misdemeanours in THAT court, on a showing made in open court of (i) rehabilitation, (ii) good conduct for two years since the last conviction in ANY court, and (iii) that the best interest of society would be served. The two-year clock runs from the last conviction in any court, not merely in the petitioned court, so a criminal-history check rather than self-report is required. Each court expunges only its own misdemeanours, so a participant with convictions in two municipal courts needs two petitions. The order does not apply to the confid

tracks.legalName: Expungement After Nonadjudication (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-15-26)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Under § 99-15-26 the court withholds acceptance of a guilty plea and sentence, imposes conditions, and on successful completion directs that the cause be dismissed and the case closed. Expungement of the resulting record is available on petition under the section's expungement subsection, which the retained review identifies as § 99-15-26(5). The complete text was obtained on this pass. Subsection (1)(a) excludes crimes against the person, a crime of violence as defined in § 97-3-2, a violation of § 97-11-31, and crimes in which a person unlawfully takes, obtains or misappropriates funds received by or entrusted to them by virtue of public office or employment; subsection (1)(d) additionally excludes trafficking under § 41-29-139(f) and every offence under the Implied Consent Law, which can only be nonadjudicated under § 63-11-30, and makes the benefit ONCE-ONLY. Subsection (4) makes the dismissal automatic on successful completion, and the expungement subsection is (5), which requires a petition. The routing question is live and unresolved: whether a successful nonadjudication dismissal requires its own § 99-15-26 petition, qualifies independently under § 99-19-71(4) as a case that was dismissed, or permits either route. tracks.legalName: Automatic Non-Conviction Removal for Post-July-2017 Dispositions (Mont. Code Ann. § 44-5-202(8))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 44-5-202(8), as amended by Ch. 321, L. 2017 effective 1 July 2017 and read with § 44-5-213(2), underpins a DOJ practice of removing non-conviction arrest data without any participant request. The Montana Department of Justice states on its Non-Conviction Removal and Sealing page that after 1 July 2017 CRISS will automatically remove all non-conviction arrest data per § 44-5-202 and that NO Record Removal Form is required. The trigger is the court's report of the disposition to the state repository, which the statute requires within fourteen business days. Relief is mandatory and automatic, there is no waiting period and no case-count limit, and there is no petition, application, motion or form for a participant to submit. The only practical question on this route is whether a record that has not been removed is ineligible or is simply the product of a court that failed to report the disposition, which is a records problem rather than a legal one.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Strike Plea or Verdict, Dismiss Charge, and Seal Case After a Completed Deferred Imposition (Mont. Code Ann. § 46-18-204)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 46-18-204 has two limbs sharing one process, one destination, one document set and one legal effect, differing only on whether relief is mandatory. Under § 46-18-204(1)(a), on a FELONY deferred imposition, after termination of the deferral period or upon termination of the time remaining under § 46-18-208, the court SHALL strike the plea of guilty or nolo contendere or the verdict of guilty and order the charge dismissed, PROVIDED THAT a petition for revocation under § 46-18-203 has not been filed. Under § 46-18-204(1)(b), on a MISDEMEANOUR deferred imposition, upon motion of the court, the defendant or the defendant's attorney, the court MAY allow withdrawal of the plea or strike the verdict and order dismissal — discretionary, with no statutory factors. After dismissal, all records and data relating to the charge are confidential criminal justice information as defined in § 44-5-103, and public access may be obtained only by district court order upon good cause shown. This is sealing, not expungement: the record is not destroyed, and per DOJ the agencies listed in § 44-5-103 retain access to the sealed record in its entirety, DOJ specifically naming law enforcement including the military and Border Patrol. tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Misdemeanor Records (Mont. Code Ann. tit. 46, ch. 18, pt. 11)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Title 46, chapter 18, part 11 lets a person petition a district court to expunge the records of one or more misdemeanour convictions entered in Montana state courts, whether in one court or several and whether in one case or several (§ 46-18-1104(1)). The petition is once in a lifetime: a person who has already had records expunged under the part, or who has already petitioned, may not petition again (§ 46-18-1104(1) and (2)). Venue is a district court in a judicial district where at least one of the convictions occurred (§ 46-18-1105), so a participant with convictions in several districts chooses among them. Section 46-18-1106(1) requires notice to every prosecution office that prosecuted an offence for which expungement is requested, and § 46-18-1106(2) gives that office fourteen days from receiving the petition to attempt to notify any victim. tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Under § 16-12-113(5)(a) a person who has COMPLETED a sentence for an act that is now permitted under Title 16, chapter 12, or that is now punishable by a lesser sentence under that chapter than the person was awarded, may petition for expungement of the conviction or for redesignation of the conviction as a misdemeanour or as a civil infraction. Section 16-12-113(5)(b) requires service on the county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed — the statute keys service to the county of FILING, not the county of prosecution. Section 16-12-113(6) directs the court to presume the petitioner satisfies the criteria unless the county attorney provides the court with a reasonable basis on which the petitioner does not; the 2021 amendment lowered that prosecutorial burden from clear and convincing evidence to providing a reasonable basis. Once the criteria are satisfied the court shall redesignate or expunge. Section 16-12-113(7) provides that unless requested by the applicant, no hearing is necessary. Section 16-12-113(8) provides that a felony conviction designated as a misdemeanour or civil infraction must be considered a misdemeanour or civil infraction for all purposes, and a misdemeanour designated as a civil infraction must be considered a civil infraction for all purposes. tracks.legalName: Non-Conviction Record Removal Request to DOJ CRISS (Mont. Code Ann. § 44-5-202(8))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Montana distinguishes removal, where the record is deleted from the database and hard copy destroyed, from sealing under § 46-18-204, where the record persists but is confidential. Section 44-5-202(8), read with § 44-5-213(2), compels the disposition to be reported to the state repository within fourteen business days, requires photographs and fingerprints to be returned to the originating agency which shall expunge all copies, and provides that a criminal justice agency may not maintain any copies. DOJ publishes a single agency form, the Expungement/Removal Request Form, with a dedicated Non-Conviction Removal request type, and its published list of eligible dispositions is charges dismissed, deferred prosecution dismissed, acquitted, charges dropped and charges not filed; in statute the categories are released without the filing of charges, charges that did not result in a conviction, and a conviction later invalidated. Two gaps must be recorded rather than papered over. First, § 44-5-202 is titled Photographs and fingerprints and subsection (8) by its terms compels expungement of PHOTOGRAPHS AND FINGERPRINTS; it does not on its face compel deletion of the criminal history record entry itself, and § 44-5-212 separately limits expunging, purging or destroying criminal justice information. DOJ nonetheless treats § 44-5-202(8) as the authority for removing non-conviction arrest

tracks.legalName: Deferred Imposition of Sentence: Automatic Withdrawal, Dismissal and Sealing, and the Fallback Motion (N.D.R.Crim.P. 32.1; N.D.C.C. §§ 12.1-32-07.1, 12.1-32-07.2)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: N.D.R.Crim.P. 32.1 makes it a mandatory term of every order deferring imposition of sentence that, sixty-one days after probation expires or terminates, the guilty plea is withdrawn or the verdict set aside, the case is dismissed and the file is sealed. Since the amendment effective 1 March 2019 the rule applies in all cases, not only misdemeanors and infractions. Where the term did not operate, the defendant may move under N.D.C.C. § 12.1-32-07.1, which also permits the court, on application by the defendant, to reduce a felony to a misdemeanor before dismissing. A deferred disposition remains pleadable in a later prosecution under § 12.1-32-02(4) and counts as a conviction for firearm purposes under § 62.1-02-01(2).

The summary marijuana process uses SFN 61663 and covers misdemeanor convictions for possession of marijuana, ingestion of marijuana and possession of marijuana paraphernalia. A pardon removes punishment but does not remove the fact of the conviction unless the certificate of pardon says so, and the form warns in terms that a pardon request will not expunge a criminal history record.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Human-Trafficking-Victim Vacatur and Sealing (N.D.C.C. § 12.1-41-14)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: An individual convicted of a listed offence committed as a direct result of being a victim of trafficking may apply by motion to vacate the conviction and seal the record. The motion, any hearing and any relief are governed by the Uniform Post-Conviction Procedure Act. Official documentation of victim status is not required, but documentation from a federal, state, local or tribal agency creates a presumption that participation was a direct result of victimisation.

tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person arrested due to the error of a law enforcement agency may file a petition with the district court. The court may order the criminal history record information related to the arrest expunged on clear and convincing evidence that the arrest was due to agency error. This is the only Nebraska adult mechanism that uses the word expunge, and product copy may use it here and nowhere else.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Firearm-Rights Restoration (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 83-1,130(2))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Firearm rights removed by a conviction are restored through the Board of Pardons process, and the judiciary states that the Board may grant a pardon with or without restoring gun rights. No standalone statewide restoration application exists. A set-aside does not restore firearm rights: § 29-2264(6) preserves the conviction for the firearm statute and § 29-2264(5)(c) requires the set-aside order itself to tell the participant to consult an attorney about firearm effects.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Immigration Consequences
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Immigration consequences are governed by federal law and no Nebraska mechanism reaches them. A Nebraska set-aside is a state-law nullification and must never be represented as having federal or immigration effect: § 29-2264(6) preserves the conviction for numerous purposes.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Juvenile Record Sealing (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 43-2,108.01 to 43-2,108.05)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Nebraska seals juvenile records automatically where no charges were filed, where charges were filed and dismissed, where diversion, mediation, restorative justice, probation or treatment was completed, or where an adjudication was followed by satisfactory completion. Where automatic sealing does not apply, the juvenile or a parent or guardian may move to seal in the court of record once the person reaches majority or six months after the case closes, whichever comes first. Sealed juvenile records are deemed never to have occurred.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Removal of Non-Conviction Records from the Public Record (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-3523(3))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Criminal history record information about an arrest, citation in lieu of arrest or referral for prosecution becomes confidential by operation of law on the timetables in § 29-3523(3), and a criminal justice agency must then respond to a public inquiry as if there were no such information. Under § 29-3523(8) the person cannot be questioned about the offence in any application for employment, bonding, licence, education or other right or privilege, in any appearance as a witness or in any other public inquiry, and may answer as if the offence never occurred.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Federal, Out-of-State and Tribal Records
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: No Nebraska court or agency can clear a federal, out-of-state or tribal record. Relief, if any, lies under the law of the sovereign that holds it. This node exists so that jurisdiction is established at intake, before any Nebraska packet is quoted or generated.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Nebraska Board of Pardons Clemency (Neb. Const. art. IV, § 13; Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 83-1,126 to 83-1,134)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: The Nebraska Board of Pardons, composed of the Governor, the Attorney General and the Secretary of State, grants pardons. A pardon nullifies the conviction, is the only route to firearm-rights restoration, and is the prerequisite to sealing a pardoned conviction. The judiciary publishes the Board's waiting periods as ten years for felonies and three years for misdemeanors, restarting on any contact with law enforcement or additional conviction, and records that the Board will not consider pardons for traffic violations, driving under the influence, or driving under suspension.

tracks.legalName: Routing of Actual-Innocence and Post-Conviction Litigation (Nebraska Postconviction Act)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Vacating a conviction is a fundamentally different remedy from clearing a record. A set-aside concedes the conviction and nullifies its civil effects; post-conviction relief attacks its validity. The Nebraska Postconviction Act provides a participant-facing verified motion, which is a distinct remedy class from record clearing.

tracks.legalName: Action to Compel Compliance With the Criminal History Record Information Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-3528)

Venue is statutory: the district court of any district in which the records involved are located, or the district court of Lancaster County. This is the route State v. Coble identifies as correct, in contrast to a motion in the criminal case.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Annulment of a Non-Conviction Disposed of On or After January 1, 2019 (RSA 651:5, II-a(a))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: New Hampshire calls this annulment, not expungement or sealing. Where a person is found not guilty on all charges that resulted from the arrest, or the case is dismissed or not prosecuted, and the offence was disposed of on or after January 1, 2019, the arrest record and court record shall be annulled thirty days after the finding if no appeal is taken under RSA 606:10, or on final determination of an appeal affirming the dismissal. There is no petition, no fee, no hearing and nothing to file. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.

tracks.mechanismExcerpt: New Hampshire calls this annulment of the record of arrest, conviction and sentence. Paragraph VIII dismisses a non-qualifying petition without a hearing, and paragraph IV then bars a further petition for three years. tracks.legalName: Expungement of Records of Arrests and Charges Not Resulting in Conviction (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-6)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Records of an arrest, charge and related proceedings that did not result in conviction may be expunged at any time, with no waiting period. Where the case was dismissed or the person was acquitted on all counts, New Jersey Courts states that the court can order an immediate expungement. There is no filing fee. tracks.legalName: Automatic Expungement of Cannabis Arrest and Conviction Records, and the Administrative Office of the Courts Verification and Expedited-Request Procedure (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-8)
authority: Cannabis Regulation Act, NMSA 1978, Sections 26-2C-1 to 26-2C-42
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person was charged with a cannabis offence that is no longer a crime on June 29, 2021, or that would have resulted in a lesser offence had the Cannabis Regulation Act been in effect, all public records held by a court or a state or local agency relating to the arrest or conviction are automatically expunged two years after the conviction date, or two years after the arrest date if there was no conviction. For a person under eighteen at the time, the records are retained for two years or until they turn eighteen, whichever comes first, and are then automatically expunged. Automatic expungement applies to public records involving only cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges and requires destruction of the records. The Administrative Office of the Courts must implement a procedure allowing eligible people to verify whether automatic expungement has occurred and to request expedited automatic expungement where it has not; where an arrest or conviction involved cannabis and non-cannabis charges, the person may request expungement of the eligible cannabis charges through that same AOC procedure. Requests to the AOC remain confidential and are not subject to disclosure. There is no court petition on this track: Rule 1-077.1(A) NMRA now excepts cannabis records from the expungement rule, former Rule 1-077.1(B)(4) was deleted and Form 4-954 NMRA was withdrawn, all effective

tracks.legalName: Dismissal of Sentence, Vacatur and Redesignation for Cannabis Convictions (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-9)
authority: Cannabis Regulation Act, NMSA 1978, Sections 26-2C-1 to 26-2C-42
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A correctional facility, county jail or juvenile correctional facility holding a person for a cannabis offence that is no longer a crime, or that would have been a lesser offence had the Cannabis Regulation Act been in effect, was required to notify the court that the case may be reopened for dismissal of the sentence or expunged. The court must reopen the case and dismiss the sentence if it is legally invalid. A person who has completed such a sentence is entitled to have the conviction dismissed and expunged as legally invalid, or redesignated as a penalty assessment citation. The Department of Public Safety was to identify potentially eligible past convictions and notify the corrections department, prosecutors and defence counsel, and prosecutors had until July 1, 2022 to decide whether to challenge a dismissal, expungement or redesignation. This is sentence relief and vacatur, not record clearing, and it turns on a legal-invalidity analysis.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge Arrest Records and Public Records upon Conviction (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-5)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person convicted of a municipal ordinance violation, misdemeanor or felony may, after completing the sentence and paying any fines or fees owed to the state for that conviction, petition the district court in the county of conviction to expunge the arrest records and public records related to it. Relief is discretionary. The court must find no other charge or proceeding pending, that justice will be served, that victim restitution ordered in connection with the conviction has been fulfilled, and that no other criminal conviction has occurred during a waiting period of two to ten years measured by offence class from the last date the petitioner completed a sentence in any jurisdiction. Five categories of offence are excluded outright. Three responding parties are served, the objection window is sixty days, the notice of completion of briefing must be filed before any hearing, and Rule 1-077.1(J) NMRA requires a hearing on this track in every case.

tracks.legalName: Removal of a Record from the Central Repository After a Favourable Disposition (NRS 179A.160)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: NRS 179A.160 has now been read in full and it is not a route on which nothing is filed. Subsection 1 provides that where a person has been arrested or issued a citation, or has been the subject of a warrant for alleged criminal conduct, and is acquitted or the disposition of the charge is favourable to the person, then "at any time after the charge is dismissed, acquittal is entered or disposition of the charge in favor of the person is final, the person who is the subject of a record of criminal history relating to the arrest, citation or warrant may apply in writing to the Central Repository and the agency which maintains the record to have it removed from the files which are available and generally searched for the purpose of responding to inquiries concerning the criminal history of a person." Subsection 2 makes removal mandatory — "The Central Repository and the agency shall remove the record unless" one of five stated conditions applies. So the participant makes a written application, to two recipients, with no waiting period and no hearing, and the agencies must act unless an exclusion bites. It remains a repository remedy rather than a court sealing order, so it sits alongside the NRS 179.255 petition rather than replacing it, and subsection 3 preserves a court's separate authority to order deletion or modification of a record. tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal Records After Conviction (NRS 179.245)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person convicted in Nevada may petition the court in which they were convicted to seal all records relating to the conviction once the waiting period for the offence category has run. The periods are ten years for a category A felony, a crime of violence or residential burglary; five years for a category B, C or D felony; two years for a category E felony or a gross misdemeanour; seven years for non-felony Medicaid fraud, non-felony DUI or non-felony battery constituting domestic violence; two years for misdemeanour battery, harassment, stalking or a protective-order violation; and one year for any other misdemeanour. The trigger differs by paragraph: paragraphs (a) to (d) run from release from actual custody or discharge from parole or probation, whichever is later, while paragraphs (e) to (g) run from release from actual custody or from the end of a suspended sentence, whichever is later, and the eligibility engine must model both. NRS 179.2445 creates a rebuttable presumption that records should be sealed where the applicant satisfies all statutory requirements, except for a defendant dishonourably discharged from probation under NRS 176A.850, and if the prosecutor stipulates or fails to object within 30 days the court may seal without a hearing. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expung

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Records After Decriminalization of an Offence (NRS 179.271)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: NRS 179.271, "Sealing of records after decriminalization of offense", provides a route where the conduct underlying a Nevada record is no longer a crime. The controlling review records the instrument as a written request rather than a full petition and classifies the track as custom_pleading on that basis. The section's presence and official title were confirmed in the chapter index at the Nevada Legislature; its text was not reproduced in the review. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

tracks.legalName: Sealing After Dismissal Under a Deferred Judgment (NRS 176.211)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: NRS 176.211 governs deferral of judgment and its own sealing. tracks.legalName: Consolidated Petition to Seal More Than One Record in District Court (NRS 179.2595)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: NRS 179.2595 permits a person seeking to seal more than one record to petition the district court for the county, which may seal all the records within that county including justice and municipal court cases. This is a venue overlay on the conviction and non-conviction tracks rather than a separate remedy: each underlying record still has to satisfy its own section. Clark County practice illustrates both the value and the trap: only one petition, affidavit and order is required to seal all records within the county, but the district attorney will not stipulate to petitions that include municipal court matters, so the packet must go to the appropriate city attorney and then to the district attorney with a separate signature line for each prosecuting agency. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of a Case Terminated in the Defendant's Favour (CPL § 160.50)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a criminal action terminates in the defendant's favour — a dismissal, an acquittal, a declination to prosecute, an adjournment in contemplation of dismissal that is then dismissed, or a vacated or overturned conviction — the record is sealed by direction of the court at disposition. There is no waiting period, no application and nothing to file. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. A sealed record does not appear on background checks run by employers, housing providers and other non-law-enforcement entities, and the person may generally answer that they have no criminal record. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities permitted or required to run fingerprint-based background checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider sealed records; to the New York State Education Department for hiring, discipline and licensing; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and a sealed conviction still counts as a predicate for sentence enhancement in a later case. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.

Crimes arising from a single criminal transaction may be treated as one conviction, and expunged marijuana convictions do not count toward the limit. tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Convictions for the marijuana offences described in CPL § 160.50(3)(k) are vacated, dismissed and expunged by operation of law under § 160.50(5)(a). That stage is automatic: there is no waiting period, no motion, no fee and nothing for the participant to file, and under § 160.50(5)(b)(i) the chief administrator of the courts notifies the Division of Criminal Justice Services and the heads of all appropriate police departments, district attorneys' offices and other law enforcement agencies, who mark the records as expunged. tracks.legalName: Expungement of Conviction Records (ORC 2953.32)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: The same section carries a second, stronger remedy on a different clock. The felony expungement clock is not ten years from discharge: it is ten years from the date the person first becomes eligible to apply for sealing for that felony, which is itself one, three or more years after discharge, so the calculation is compound and must be encoded as such rather than as a flat ten years. Expungement destroys, deletes and erases, subject to the statutory exceptions, but for conviction expungements the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.

tracks.legalName: Sealing or Expungement After a Not Guilty Finding, Dismissal, Grand Jury No Bill or Pardon (ORC 2953.33)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person is found not guilty by a jury or a court, is named in a dismissed complaint, indictment or information, has a no bill entered by a grand jury, or receives a Governor's pardon, the person may apply to seal or expunge the official records. A not-guilty finding or a dismissal may be applied for at any time after the entry is made upon the minutes of the court or the journal, whichever occurs first; a no bill requires the expiration of two years after the foreperson or deputy foreperson reported it; a pardon may be applied for after the pardon or after its conditions are met. Each of these is expressly subject to ORC 2953.61. tracks.legalName: Motion to Set Aside the Record After an Acquittal (ORS 137.225(1)(d))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: At any time after an acquittal, an arrested, cited or charged person may apply to the court in the county in which the person was arrested, cited or charged for an order setting aside the record of the arrest, citation or charge. There is no waiting period and, under ORS 137.225(9), no time limit for making an application. Under ORS 137.225(3)(b) the court shall grant a motion under this paragraph. Oregon calls it a set-aside and there are no separate sealing and expungement tracks: the court sets aside and seals, and under ORS 137.225(4) the conviction, arrest, citation, charge or other proceeding is deemed not to have occurred and the person may answer accordingly any questions relating to its occurrence. The order reaches Oregon court and law enforcement records including the Oregon State Police LEDS system. It does not reach federal or other states' records. Under 2024 Oregon State Police policy a set-aside does not restore firearm rights; a separate restoration process is required. The enacted text splits contempt across two tiers. A finding of a person in contempt of court for violating an order related to abuse or a person crime sits in the five-year tier alongside Class C felonies. A finding of contempt not so described sits in the one-year tier alongside Class B and C misdemeanors and violations. Each runs from the date of the finding or the release from imprisonment for the finding sought to be set aside, whichever is later. ORS 137.225(13)(b) defines "order related to abuse or a person crime" as a court order issued under ORS 107.095(1)(c) or (d), 107.700 to 107.735, 124.005 to 124.040, 133.035, 135.247 or 163.760 to 163.777, or a court order arising from a criminal case involving a sex crime, stalking under ORS 163.732, or a person felony or person Class A misdemeanor committed against the person's family or household member as defined in ORS 135.230. Oregon calls it a set-aside and there are no separate sealing and expungement tracks: the court sets aside and seals, and under ORS 137.225(4) the conviction, arrest, citation, charge or other proceeding is deemed not to have occurred and the person may answer accordingly any questions relating to its occurrence. A person still under supervision as part of that sentence has not fully complied. The tiers run seven years for a Class B felony, five years for a Class C felony, three years for a Class A misdemeanor and one year for a Class B or C misdemeanor or a violation, each measured from the date of conviction or the release from imprisonment for the conviction sought to be set aside, whichever is later. Where the court has reduced the offence classification the applicable period is the one associated with the reduced classification. tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Non-Conviction Summary Case Records Pursuant to Pa.R.Crim.P. 490
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Rule 490 governs expungement in summary cases. Any case in which a summary offense was filed together with a misdemeanor, felony or murder charge proceeds under Rule 790 instead. The rule prescribes the petition contents, the attached Pennsylvania State Police criminal history report obtained within 60 days before filing, service on the attorney for the Commonwealth, and the expungement order.

scopedOutStatements.text: The case included a misdemeanour, felony or murder charge alongside the summary offences, which routes it to Rule 790.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of a Qualifying Underage Alcohol Conviction Under 18 Pa.C.S. § 6308
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person who is 21 years of age or older was convicted of violating § 6308 for the purchase, consumption, possession or transportation of liquor or malt or brewed beverages, and has satisfied all terms and conditions of the sentence, the court shall order expungement of the record of the conviction.

scopedOutStatements.text: The participant is under 21.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Non-Conviction Records Pursuant to Pa.R.Crim.P. 790
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 9122(a) requires expungement of criminal history record information where no disposition has been received or recorded within 18 months after the date of arrest and the court finds the conditions met, or where a court order requires nonconviction data to be expunged. Rule 790 prescribes the petition contents, the attached Pennsylvania State Police criminal history report, service on the attorney for the Commonwealth, and the expungement order for court cases.

scopedOutStatements.text: Fines, costs or restitution remain unpaid, because Rule 790 requires the payment status to be stated.
Expungement under § 9122 is not limited access. Consumer-facing copy must keep the two remedies distinct and must never tell a participant the record no longer exists beyond what § 9122.5 permits.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Order for Limited Access Under 18 Pa.C.S. § 9122.1
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 9122.1(a) permits a petition for limited access to a qualifying misdemeanour or ungraded offence carrying a maximum penalty of no more than five years where the person has been free from conviction for a period of seven years, has completed all court-ordered restitution, and has paid the authorized fee. Section 9122.1(a.1), added by Act 36 of 2023, extends the petition to qualifying felonies other than felonies of the first and second degree where the person has been free from conviction for a period of ten years on the same conditions. Rule 791 prescribes the petition, the attached Pennsylvania State Police criminal history report obtained within 60 days before filing, service on the attorney for the Commonwealth, and the order.

scopedOutStatements.text: The offence appears on the § 9122.1(b) exclusion list.
The prior record may trigger the § 9122.1(b)(2) disqualifiers, including the serious-offence-within-15-years and two-or-more-offences-within-10-years rules.

tracks.legalName: Clean Slate Automatic Limited Access Under 18 Pa.C.S. § 9122.2
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 9122.2 provides automatic limited access without any petition. Subsection (a)(1) reaches a conviction of a misdemeanour of the second degree or a misdemeanour punishable by no more than two years where the person has been free for seven years from conviction for any offence punishable by imprisonment of one or more years. Subsection (a)(1.1) reaches a qualifying offence on the same terms after ten years. Subsection (a)(2) reaches charges resulting in a final disposition other than a conviction. Subsection (a)(3) reaches a summary conviction when five years have elapsed since entry of the judgment of conviction. Subsection (a)(4) reaches a conviction for which a conditional pardon was granted. Under subsection (b) the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts transmits eligible records to the Pennsylvania State Police central repository and removes records for which a notification of ineligibility is received.
officialFormRefs: 18 Pa.C.S. § 9122.2 (Clean slate limited access), current official text

scopedOutStatements.text: Any § 9122.3 exclusion applies to the record.

Limited access is not expungement. Records subject to limited access remain available to criminal justice agencies, are disclosed to a court for sentencing, and must be self-disclosed for public-office eligibility under § 9122.5.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Expungement Following Complete Acquittal
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person is acquitted of all charges based on the same conduct or arising from the same criminal episode, § 9122(a) provides for expungement without a petition. The Commonwealth has 60 days to object and, where the statutory requirements are met, expungement occurs no later than 12 months from the date of acquittal.

scopedOutStatements.text: Do not offer this track for a partial acquittal. Section 9122(a) reaches acquittal of all charges based on the same conduct or arising from the same criminal episode.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement on Age 70 or Death Grounds
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 9122(b) permits a court to order expungement where the person reaches 70 years of age and has been free of arrest or prosecution for ten years following final release from confinement or supervision, or where the person has been dead for three years.

scopedOutStatements.text: Any arrest or prosecution during the ten years following final release, on the age-70 ground.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of the Arrest Record on Successful Completion of Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: When the judge orders dismissal of the charges after successful completion of Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition, Rule 320 provides that the judge also shall order expungement of the defendant's arrest record, subject to a Commonwealth objection filed within 30 days after service of the motion for dismissal, on which the Commonwealth must show compelling reasons to retain the record. Section 9122(b.1) removes the court's authority to expunge the arrest record where ARD was granted for enumerated sexual offences and the victim was under 18.

scopedOutStatements.text: The ARD offence was a sexual offence with a victim under 18, where § 9122(b.1) removes the court's authority to expunge the arrest record.
Do not offer this track where ARD was granted for an enumerated sexual offence with a victim under 18. Section 9122(b.1) removes the court's authority to expunge the arrest record.

tracks.legalName: Expungement Following an Unconditional Pardon
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A pardon is executive clemency and does not by itself erase the record. Where an unconditional pardon has been granted, § 9122 provides for expungement: the Board of Pardons transmits eligible records to the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts quarterly, the AOPC sends the record to the court of common pleas, and the court orders expungement after confirming the criteria. A conditional pardon may instead trigger Clean Slate limited access under § 9122.2(a)(4).

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of a Summary Conviction After Five Arrest-Free Years
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 9122(b) permits a court to order expungement of a summary offence conviction where the person has been free of arrest or prosecution for five years following the conviction. The petition is made on the Rule 490 or Rule 790 form depending on the court in which the case was disposed.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Commercial Sexual Activity Records (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-34.1-5)

Laws § 12-10-12 for violations of § 11-34.1-2 or § 11-34.1-4 may be expunged one year after completion of sentence, and the court may grant the motion regardless of first-offender status. The one-year period and the waiver of first-offender status make this route materially more generous than the general Chapter 12-1.3 tracks.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Expunge an Offence Decriminalized After Conviction (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 12-1.3-2(g), 12-1.3-3(e))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Separate from the marijuana route, a person may file for expungement of an offence that was decriminalized after the date of conviction. The court holds a hearing and may require the petitioner to demonstrate that the prior conviction would qualify as a decriminalized offence under current Rhode Island law, which may be done by the petitioner's own affidavit. Where the conditions of the original sentence are complete and required fines, fees and costs are paid in full, the court orders the expungement without cost to the petitioner. There is no waiting period.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Expunge Records of a Completed Deferred Sentence (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 12-19-19, 12-1.3-2(e))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person who received a deferred sentence may move for expungement after completion of the deferred sentence. If the court finds after a hearing that the person complied with all terms of the deferral agreement, including payment of fines, fees, costs, assessments and restitution, the person becomes immediately eligible for consideration for expungement. There is no waiting period beyond completion. The court must also find no pending criminal proceedings and good moral character, and no person convicted of a crime of violence may have deferred-sentence records expunged. A deferred sentence is not an automatic expungement: the court process and the hearing are still required.

Relief is discretionary on findings of good moral character, rehabilitation to the court's satisfaction, and consistency with the public interest.

tracks.legalName: Non-Conviction Sealing and Destruction of Identification Records (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 12-1-12, 12-1-12.1)
authority: R.I. Dist. Ct. R. Crim. P. 48(a)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: For acquittals, dismissals, no true bills, no informations and other exonerations, identification records such as fingerprints, photographs, physical measurements and other arrest identification records must generally be destroyed within 60 days, and court records are sealed consistent with § 12-1-12.1. District Court Rule 48(a) dismissals on or after 1 January 2023 are sealed automatically by the court not less than 10 and not more than 20 days after dismissal; Rule 48(a) dismissals before that date are sealed administratively by the clerk at the defendant's request, with the order sent electronically to BCI and carried out within 90 days of receipt. The route runs through the Solicitor's Office.
