tracks.legalName: Solicitor Application to Expunge an Old Unlawful Handgun Possession Conviction, S.C. Code § 17-1-65
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 17-1-65 provides that a person may apply for an expungement of one conviction for unlawful possession of a handgun as provided in § 16-23-20, if the conviction occurred prior to the enactment of the South Carolina Constitutional Carry/Second Amendment Preservation Act of 2024, and that an application under the section must be made within five years of the enactment of the section. The section was created by 2024 Act No. 111 (H.3594), § 20, effective March 7, 2024, which fixes both dates: the conviction must predate March 7, 2024, and the application must be made before March 7, 2029. SCCA 223C (06/2024), read at source on the same date, is the instrument for this route and not a general-purpose General Sessions destruction order: it recites that the defendant is entitled to have the records expunged 'according to S.C. Code Ann. § 17-1-65' and carries three findings tracking the section exactly — conviction under § 16-23-20 prior to the enactment of the Act on March 7, 2024; application submitted prior to March 7, 2029; and no previous application for expungement of a handgun possession conviction under § 17-1-65. The form also recites the § 17-1-40 sealed retentions and the § 22-5-910 SLED nonpublic retention, so the surviving records are stated on the order itself. This is a closing window and the deadline should be surfaced unprompted.

tracks.legalName: Summary Court Expungement of a Non-Conviction, S.C. Code § 17-22-950
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 17-22-950 splits on a single fact: whether the accused person was fingerprinted. tracks.legalName: Automatic Removal of Non-Felony Charges or Convictions from the Public Record (SDCL § 23A-3-34)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Any charge or conviction resulting from a case where a petty offense, municipal ordinance violation or a Class 2 misdemeanor was the highest charged offense shall be automatically removed from a defendant's public record after five years if all court-ordered conditions on the case have been satisfied and the defendant has not been convicted of any further offenses within those five years. The case record remains available to court personnel or as authorized by order of the court and may be used as an enhancement in the prosecution of subsequent offenses as provided by law.

scopedOutStatements.text: A case where the highest charge exceeded a Class 2 misdemeanor.

Records removed under § 23A-3-34 remain available to court personnel or by order of the court and may be used as an enhancement in the prosecution of subsequent offences. Never say that automatic removal of a Class 2 misdemeanor means the record can never be used again.

Before § 23A-3-34 was enacted in 2016, executive pardon was the only mechanism to seal a conviction record from public view in South Dakota. That history explains why the state's conviction relief is so thin and is useful in participant conversations.

tracks.legalName: Motion for Expungement of Arrest Record (SDCL §§ 23A-3-26 to 23A-3-32)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: An arrested person may apply to the court that would have jurisdiction over the crime for which the person was arrested for an order expunging the record of the arrest: after one year from the arrest where no accusatory instrument was filed; after one year from the date the prosecuting attorney formally dismisses the entire criminal case on the record; at any time after an acquittal; or within one year of a formal dismissal of the entire case on a showing of compelling necessity. The motion starts a new civil action, may be made only on a record of arrest, and more than one arrest record requires a separate case for each. The court may enter the order only after finding by clear and convincing evidence that the ends of justice and the best interests of the public and the defendant or arrested person will be served. Expungement in South Dakota means sealing, not destruction, and a nonpublic disposition record is retained by the Division of Criminal Investigation.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Records on the Grant of a Chapter 24-14 Pardon (SDCL § 24-14-11)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person granted a pardon under the provisions of chapter 24-14 is released from all disabilities consequent on the conviction. Upon the granting of such a pardon the Governor shall order that all official records relating to the pardoned person's arrest, indictment or information, trial, finding of guilt, application for a pardon, and the proceedings of the Board of Pardons and Paroles be sealed. The Governor files a public document with the secretary of state certifying the pardon; that document remains public for five years and is then sealed. A pardon granted without following the provisions of the chapter may not be sealed. The pardon restores the person to their pre-arrest status and protects against perjury or false-statement liability for failing to acknowledge the matter, but the conviction may still be considered for sentencing on subsequent offences and habitual-offender determinations.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Records on Discharge and Dismissal after a Suspended Imposition of Sentence (SDCL §§ 23A-27-13 to 23A-27-17)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: For certain offenses a court may suspend imposition of sentence where the person has never before been convicted of a felony. After the person completes all court conditions the defendant is discharged and the case is dismissed without adjudication of guilt, and the discharge and dismissal are not deemed a conviction for disqualifications or disabilities imposed by law. Upon the discharge and dismissal a court SHALL order that all official records, other than the nonpublic records retained by the Division of Criminal Investigation, be sealed along with all records relating to the arrest, indictment or information, trial, finding of guilt, and dismissal and discharge. The order restores the person to the status occupied before arrest, indictment or information, and the person is not guilty of perjury or of giving a false statement for failing to recite or acknowledge the matter.

tracks.legalName: Immediate expunction order on acquittal in open court, T.C.A. § 40-32-106
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: On a not-guilty verdict by judge or jury on all counts, the presiding judge must ask the acquitted person whether they want the records removed and destroyed, and if the answer is yes the court issues the order immediately with no separate petition. The section was renumbered by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24: the acquittal ground that sat at former § 40-32-101(a) is now within § 40-32-106, whose non-conviction grounds include a verdict of not guilty, and which carries the acquittal-in-open-court procedure. No fee may be charged: § 40-32-106(a)(1) provides that qualifying public records must be removed and destroyed without cost to the person. Under § 40-32-110 expunction restores the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction.

A person whose arrest record exists but for whom the court with jurisdiction over the offence for which the person was arrested has no history of the arrest within the court's records. This is the participant whose arrest never produced a court file — the case that the § 40-32-106 route cannot reach, because that route runs to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action and here there is no previous action in that court's records. tracks.legalName: Expunction of a conviction for illegal registration or voting, T.C.A. § 40-32-107(c) with procedure at § 40-32-108
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Expunction of the conviction record. Under T.C.A. § 40-32-110 the petitioner is entitled to have all public records of the expunged conviction destroyed in the manner set out in the chapter, restoring the person in contemplation of law to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction. A person convicted of illegal registration or voting under T.C.A. § 2-19-107, where fifteen years have elapsed since completion of the sentence, every sentence requirement has been fulfilled, the offence occurred prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence, and the person has not previously been granted expunction under § 40-32-107(a), (b) or (c). tracks.legalName: Expunction after successful completion of judicial diversion, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(d) and § 40-35-313
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Judicial diversion under T.C.A. § 40-35-313 is a conditional guilty plea with no judgment of conviction entered: the court defers adjudication and places the person on probation, typically six to eighteen months, and on successful completion discharges and dismisses the case. A completed judicial diversion is not a conviction under Tennessee law. Under § 40-32-106(d)(1) the person may then petition for expunction where the charges were dismissed as a result of successful completion of a judicial diversion programme pursuant to § 40-35-313. Public Chapter 268 amended § 40-35-313(b) and (c) to replace the old § 40-32-101 subdivision citations with references to § 40-32-101 and to title 40, chapter 32, which is the official cross-reference confirming the route survived the reorganization. The clerk's fee under § 8-21-401 applies, the TBI certificate is required, and the § 40-32-106(d)(2) sexual-offence bar applies here too. Federal systems and security-clearance background checks may still see the underlying guilty plea, which should be stated to every judicial diversion participant.

tracks.legalName: Free expunction of a non-conviction record by petition, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(a)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Created by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608 effective 2026-03-25. All public records of a person charged with a misdemeanour or felony must, upon petition by that person to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action, be removed and destroyed without cost to the person where the charge was dismissed other than by diversion completion, a no true bill was returned, the person was arrested and released without being charged, a nolle prosequi was entered, a verdict of not guilty was returned, or on the section's further grounds including qualifying implied-consent dismissals, abatement by death, mistaken identity and racial-justice-protest convictions. Subsection (a)(2) extends the same no-cost treatment to a successfully defended order of protection and to expired bonds under § 38-3-109. There is no waiting period. The TBI certificate under § 40-32-102(c) is not required for a § 40-32-106 expunction unless the expunction resulted from successful completion of pretrial or judicial diversion. Under § 40-32-110 expunction restores the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction, and under § 40-32-102(e) the expunged records are confidential and unlawful release is a Class A misdemeanour.

tracks.legalName: Expunction after successful completion of pretrial diversion, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(d)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Prosecution is suspended under a memorandum of understanding with the district attorney general; the person does not plead guilty and is not found guilty. On successful completion the charges are dismissed, and under T.C.A. § 40-32-106(d)(1) the person may then petition for expunction of the public records where the charges were dismissed as a result of successful completion of a pretrial diversion programme pursuant to §§ 40-15-102 through 40-15-107. The provision is permissive as to filing and mandatory as to nothing: a petition is required and expunction is not automatic. Section 40-32-106(d)(3) requires the appropriate clerk's fee under § 8-21-401, so unlike a straight dismissal this route is not free. Section 40-32-106(d)(2) bars expunction where the diverted offence was a sexual offence or a violent sexual offence as defined in § 40-39-202. The TBI certificate under § 40-32-102(c) is required here, because the exemption for § 40-32-106 expunctions is expressly carved back where the expunction resulted from successful completion of pretrial diversion.

tracks.legalName: Partial removal of records of charges not resulting in conviction in a mixed case, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(c)(2)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: The controlling review identified this remedy from a secondary profile and left its citation unresolved as the highest-value Tennessee research item. Whether the relief reaches paper records or only electronic databases was not established, and the review flags that limitation as materially changing what a participant gets.

tracks.legalName: Expunction of up to two offences, T.C.A. § 40-32-107(b) with procedure at § 40-32-108
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06. Section 40-32-107(b) defines an eligible petitioner as a person seeking expunction of no more than two offences. Each offence must be eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1) and must have occurred prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence, including ineligible federal and other-state convictions. The permitted combinations are exhaustive: two misdemeanours, or one felony and one misdemeanour. Two felonies are not available on this route. At filing there must be five years since completion of sentence for any misdemeanour or Class E felony being expunged and ten years for any Class C or Class D felony being expunged, every sentence requirement must be fulfilled for each offence, and the person must not previously have been granted expunction under subsection (a), this subsection (b) or subsection (c). Subsection (b)(2) provides a single-episode merger mirroring (a)(1)(F): contemporaneous same-location single-intent convictions count as a single offence for the purposes of the two-offence limit, so one episode does not consume both slots. Subsection (b)(3) directs the petitioner to § 40-32-108, so the same DA-prepared petition procedure applies. The reciprocal bars across (a), (b) and (c) are lifetime, which is why using this pathway forecloses a later second use and makes the timing decision consequential.

tracks.legalName: Expunction after trial court acquittal, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. arts. 55A.002 and 55A.201
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person tried and acquitted by the trial court is entitled to expunction. Under art. 55A.201 the order shall be entered not later than the 30th day after the date of acquittal, on request of the acquitted person after notice to the state, or on request of the attorney representing the state with the person's consent. On acquittal the trial court shall advise the person of the right to expunction. The requesting party must provide the information required in an art. 55A.253 petition. The order is prepared by the acquitted person's attorney if the person was represented, otherwise by the attorney representing the state. Where the 30-day window has closed or the court did not act, the person falls back to an ordinary ex parte petition under art. 55A.251, which lists art. 55A.002 among the qualifying entitlements. Article 55A.151 bars relief where the acquitted offence arose out of a criminal episode as defined by Penal Code 3.01 and the person was convicted of, or remains subject to prosecution for, at least one other offence in that episode. Under art. 102.0061(c), read at source on 2026-08-06, the filing fee must be waived where the expunction relates to an acquittal other than one described by art. 55A.151 and the petition is filed not later than the 30th day after the acquittal.

tracks.legalName: Discretionary expunction on appellate acquittal or prosecutor recommendation, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 55A.101
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A court may expunge where the person was convicted at trial and then acquitted by the Court of Criminal Appeals, or by a court of appeals once the period for granting discretionary review has expired, or where the office of the attorney representing the state authorised by law to prosecute the offence recommends the expunction to the court before the person is tried, whether or not a charging instrument was presented. Relief is discretionary: the court may expunge. A justice court or municipal court of record may act under the article only on fine-only arrests. Article 55A.151 bars relief where the acquitted offence arose out of a criminal episode in which the person was convicted of, or remains subject to prosecution for, another offence.

tracks.legalName: Expunction where the charge was dismissed or quashed, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. arts. 55A.051 and 55A.053
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where an indictment or information was presented and then dismissed or quashed, expunction is available if the court finds the dismissal or quashal was because the person completed a veterans treatment court programme under Government Code Chapter 124, completed a mental health court programme under Chapter 125, completed a pretrial intervention programme authorised under Government Code 76.011, the presentment was made because of mistake, false information or another similar reason indicating absence of probable cause at the time of dismissal, or the charging instrument was void. Entitlement does not depend on any limitations period, under art. 55A.053(d). A person may receive only one expunction on the veterans court ground and only one on the mental health court ground, and must file an affidavit attesting to that fact. Relief is mandatory on the findings, but the court must make the finding about why the case was dismissed, which is a real evidentiary burden: a dismissal order that simply says dismissed establishes no statutory ground.

tracks.legalName: Expunction on mistaken identity or identity theft, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. arts. 55A.006 and 55A.256
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person was arrested solely because identifying information was inaccurate due to clerical error, or another arrested person falsely gave the applicant's identifying information without consent and that deception is the only reason the applicant's information is in the records, relief is available. Article 55A.006 operates notwithstanding the art. 55A.001 arrest requirement, so the applicant need not have been arrested at all. This is not a petition. The applicant files a verified application, including authenticated fingerprint records, with the attorney representing the state in the prosecution of felonies in the county where the applicant resides or where the offence was alleged to have occurred. Article 55A.256(b) prescribes the application's contents. After verifying the allegations the prosecutor supplements missing arrest information, forwards the application to the district court with the agency list attached, and requests the order, and the court enters a final order without a hearing. The effect differs from ordinary expunction: under art. 55A.354 agencies obliterate the applicant's identifying information and substitute the arrested person's information rather than returning or destroying the file, and index references are not deleted. The S.B. 1667 anti-duplication rules apply to the application under art. 55A.256(c-1).

tracks.legalName: Expunction where no charge was filed, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. arts. 55A.051 and 55A.052
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Texas says expunction, not expungement, and the filing is an ex parte petition by a petitioner. Chapter 55A was enacted by H.B. 4504 of the 88th Legislature as a nonsubstantive revision effective 2025-01-01, replacing repealed Chapter 55, and was amended by S.B. 1667 effective 2025-09-01. Under art. 55A.052 a person arrested for a felony or misdemeanour is entitled to expunction where no indictment or information was ever presented, once the applicable period has run — 180 days for a Class C misdemeanour arrest with no felony from the same transaction, one year for a Class A or B misdemeanour arrest on the same condition, three years for a felony arrest or where a felony charge arose from the same transaction — or where the attorney representing the state certifies the records are not needed for any criminal investigation or prosecution. Entitlement exists regardless of whether a limitations period exists or has expired, under art. 55A.052(b). The art. 55A.051 threshold applies throughout: released, no final conviction, no charge pending, and no Chapter 42A community supervision other than for a Class C misdemeanour. Relief is mandatory: if the court finds entitlement it shall enter the order.

tracks.legalName: Expunction after a pardon or other relief on the basis of actual innocence, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. arts. 55A.003 and 55A.202
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person tried, convicted and then pardoned or otherwise granted relief on the basis of actual innocence, where the pardon or order says so on its face, is entitled to expunction. The order is entered not later than the 30th day after the court receives notice of the pardon or grant of relief. Under art. 55A.204 the attorney representing the state prepares the order and must notify the Texas Department of Criminal Justice if the person is in custody, and art. 55A.205 prescribes the order's content including the agency listing and specific DPS and TDCJ index-deletion directives. Under art. 55A.202(b) the person provides the information required in an art. 55A.253 petition. Confirmed on 2026-08-06 that art. 55A.251 does not list art. 55A.003 among its petition grounds, though art. 55A.252 does for a fine-only offence, so for an ordinary case the automatic-entry route is the route.

tracks.legalName: Streamlined expunction order after a specialty court dismissal, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 55A.203
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a case was dismissed following successful completion of a veterans treatment court programme under Government Code Chapter 124 or a mental health court programme under Chapter 125, a district court may, with the consent of the attorney representing the state, enter an expunction order not later than the 30th day after the dismissal or after it receives the dismissal information. Article 55A.203(c) forbids the court charging any fee or assessing any cost for such an order, and art. 102.0061(d) separately requires waiver of the district-court filing fee for an entitlement under art. 55A.053(a)(2)(A) or (B). Article 55A.203(d), added by S.B. 1667, requires the person to provide the court with the information required in an art. 55A.253 petition. A person may receive only one expunction on each ground and must file an affidavit attesting to that fact. The prosecutor's consent makes the streamlined route discretionary in practice even though the underlying art. 55A.053 entitlement is mandatory; where consent is withheld or the window closes, the ordinary petition route under art. 55A.053 remains open, because the entitlement lives there rather than in art. 55A.203. Unlike art. 55A.201, art. 55A.203 is limited to district courts.

tracks.legalName: Automatic order of nondisclosure after deferred adjudication for a nonviolent misdemeanour, Tex. Gov't Code 411.072
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06. Where a person receives a discharge and dismissal under art. 42A.111 after deferred adjudication community supervision for a misdemeanour, and satisfies Gov't Code 411.074, the court that placed the person on deferred adjudication shall issue an order of nondisclosure. The court itself determines whether the 411.074 requirements are satisfied. No petition exists and none is required: the participant's only obligations are to present to the court any evidence necessary to establish eligibility, and to pay a $28 fee to the clerk before the court issues the order. Section 411.0716(b) limits the section to a discharge and dismissal received on or after 2017-09-01. The court must issue at discharge and dismissal where that occurs on or after the 180th day after placement on deferred adjudication, and otherwise as soon as practicable on or after the 180th day. Section 411.072 is the only provision in either Texas scheme with no prosecutor role at all: no consent, no certification, no notice, no opportunity to be heard and no objection right, and the 411.0745(e) notice-and-hearing machinery applies only on receipt of a petition and so does not reach it. Where the court did not act, OCA publishes a model letter, expressly not a petition, that the person submits to the court presenting evidence of entitlement with the $28 fee. Section 411.072 was last amend

tracks.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after a misdemeanour conviction without community supervision, Tex. Gov't Code 411.0735
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person convicted of a misdemeanour who was not placed on community supervision of any kind and whose sentence is complete, and who is not eligible under Gov't Code 411.073. Under 411.0735(c-1) the court may not issue the order if it determines the offence, other than a Penal Code 22.01 offence, was violent or sexual in nature — a conviction for assault under 22.01 may still qualify. Section 411.0735 was last amended in 2017 and was not touched in 2025 or 2026.

tracks.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after deferred adjudication, felonies and certain misdemeanours, Tex. Gov't Code 411.0725
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Deferred adjudication community supervision resulting in discharge and dismissal, where the person does not qualify under Gov't Code 411.072. Read at source on 2026-08-06 the waiting periods are: on the discharge and dismissal for a misdemeanour not listed in the section's subdivision (2); the second anniversary of discharge and dismissal for a misdemeanour under Penal Code Chapters 20, 21, 22, 25, 42, 43 or 46; and the fifth anniversary of discharge and dismissal for a felony. Penal Code Chapter 71 is not on that list — it appears in the 411.072 automatic exclusions and in the 411.073 and 411.0735 offence exclusions. Unlike 411.072, a prior conviction or deferred adjudication does not by itself defeat eligibility under 411.0725(c), subject to the 411.074 bars. The court shall issue the order after notice to the state, an opportunity for a hearing, and a determination of entitlement and best interest of justice. Section 411.0725 was last amended in 2019 and was not touched in 2025 or 2026.

tracks.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after a DWI conviction without qualifying community supervision, Tex. Gov't Code 411.0736
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A conviction under Penal Code 49.04 for DWI punishable as a Class B misdemeanour, other than an offence punishable under 49.04(d), where the person does not qualify under Gov't Code 411.0731 — typically because community supervision was revoked or none was imposed. The waiting period is the third anniversary of completing the sentence where the person successfully complied with a sentence condition requiring an ignition interlock device for six months or longer, and otherwise the fifth anniversary. Section 411.0736(c) expressly requires the petition to include evidence that the person is entitled to file it. Under 411.0736(e) a court may not issue the order if the attorney representing the state presents evidence sufficient to the court that the offence resulted in a motor vehicle collision involving another person, including a passenger, regardless of injury or death. Waiver of the fine and costs by the court does not disqualify. The section was last amended in 2023 and was not touched in 2025 or 2026.

tracks.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after community supervision following a misdemeanour conviction, Tex. Gov't Code 411.073
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person convicted of a misdemeanour and placed on community supervision under a Chapter 42A provision other than Subchapter C — straight probation rather than deferred adjudication, including split sentences — who successfully completed it. The waiting period is immediate on completion of community supervision, except that a misdemeanour under Penal Code Chapters 20, 21, 22, 25, 42, 43 or 46 waits until the second anniversary of completion. Completion means the full supervision period including any term of confinement and payment of all fines, costs and restitution. This is the ordinary route for a probated misdemeanour conviction and is probably the highest-volume conviction track in the state. Section 411.073 was last amended in 2017 and was not touched in 2025 or 2026.

tracks.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after successful completion of a veterans treatment court programme, Tex. Gov't Code 411.0727
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Successful completion of a veterans treatment court programme as defined by Government Code Chapter 124 or former law. The waiting period is the second anniversary of the date of successful completion, and a felony conviction at any time during those two years defeats it. Under 411.0727(e) the section is not available where entry into the programme arose from an offence involving operating a motor vehicle while intoxicated. A prior conviction for any offence on the section's own exclusion list also defeats it. Section 411.0727 was last amended in 2017 and was not touched in 2025 or 2026. The overlap with expunction is decisive and is routing logic rather than an optimisation: a veterans treatment court dismissal may also support expunction under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 55A.053(a)(2)(A) with the streamlined 30-day order under art. 55A.203 and no fee, and expunction is the stronger remedy because it destroys rather than seals.

tracks.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after a court-approved veterans reemployment programme, Tex. Gov't Code 411.0729
authority: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. ch. 42A subch. H-1
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A misdemeanour for which the person was placed on community supervision, including deferred adjudication, who successfully completed all conditions and successfully completed a court-approved veterans reemployment programme under Code of Criminal Procedure Chapter 42A, Subchapter H-1, after committing the offence, and who is a veteran of the United States Armed Forces including reserves, national guard or state guard. Read at source on 2026-08-06: the court shall enter the order after notice to the state and a hearing on whether issuance is in the best interest of justice, and the statute names no filing party — there is no petition requirement in the section. Under 411.0729(b) the section applies regardless of whether the defendant meets the other eligibility criteria in the subchapter, so the Gov't Code 411.074 basic conditions do not gate it. There is no waiting period. OCA nonetheless publishes a model petition and instructions for the section, because in practice courts may require a petition or may not hold the hearing. tracks.legalName: Motion to reduce conviction under Utah Code 76-3-402, adjacent non-relief routing node
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: This node produces no record-clearing relief and no packet of its own. A motion to reduce a conviction, commonly called a 402 motion, is not a record-clearing mechanism, but Utah Courts routes ineligible petitioners to it and a reduction can convert an ineligible conviction into an eligible one by changing the offence level and therefore both the applicable waiting period and the conviction-counting math under 77-40a-303 and 77-40a-205. The adopted counsel structure places it in the Utah decision tree as an adjacent non-relief routing node — a not yet, but here is the path branch — and expressly not as a relief track.

tracks.legalName: Clean Slate automatic expungement of convictions, Utah Code 77-40a-205
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Every conviction in the case must be a misdemeanour for possession of a controlled substance under Subsection 58-37-8(2)(a)(i), a class B misdemeanour, a class C misdemeanour, or an infraction. The waiting periods run from the day the individual is adjudicated: five years for class C misdemeanours and infractions, six years for class B misdemeanours, and seven years for class A misdemeanour possession of a controlled substance under 58-37-8(2)(a)(i). The prosecuting agency receives notice and may object; if 35 days pass without a written objection the court proceeds. Since 2026-01-01 the court identifies eligible cases on its own initiative under 77-40a-204(3), and form 1200EX is retired. For cases adjudicated on or after 2020-05-01 that are not traffic offenses the target is expungement within 30 days of the court determining requirements are satisfied; for cases adjudicated or dismissed before that date, within one year of identification. In practice the process can take up to 120 days because the court runs the job monthly and must allow the objection window.

tracks.legalName: Automatic expungement after acquittal or dismissal with prejudice, Utah Code 77-40a-206
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person is acquitted on all charges the court expunges the case 60 days after the acquittal. Where the case is dismissed with prejudice the court expunges 180 days after the day of dismissal if no appeal was filed, or after a final non-appealable order if one was. A case dismissed with prejudice as a result of successful completion of a plea in abeyance agreement is excluded, as is a case in which the person was found not guilty by reason of insanity. Since 2026-01-01 the identification duty at 77-40a-204(3) puts the work on the court's own initiative and form 1200EX is retired. The duty is mandatory once the case is identified. Section 77-40a-204 does not preclude filing a petition for a case that is eligible for automatic expungement where the automatic expungement has not occurred, which is what makes the petition tracks a genuine fallback rather than a duplicate.

tracks.legalName: Automatic deletion of traffic offense records, Utah Code 77-40a-202
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: The court deletes traffic offense records on its own initiative. A traffic offense means an infraction or class B or C misdemeanour under Title 41 Chapter 6a, Title 53 Chapter 3 Part 2 and Title 73 Chapter 18, plus substantially similar local ordinances. Title 41 Chapter 6a Part 5, driving under the influence and reckless driving, and Sections 73-18-13 through 73-18-13.6 are expressly not traffic offenses, so DUI is not a traffic offense in Utah. Deletion follows an acquittal on all charges, a dismissal with prejudice other than one resulting from successful completion of a plea in abeyance, or adjudication plus five years for class C misdemeanours and infractions or six years for class B misdemeanours. Where the qualifying event occurred on or after 2020-05-01 the court deletes on identification; where it occurred before that date the court deletes within one year of identification. The court deletes and BCI neither receives nor indexes expunged traffic offenses, so traffic expungement enquiries go to the court rather than to BCI. The duty is mandatory.

tracks.legalName: Appellate record expungement, Utah Supreme Court Standing Order No. 12
authority: Utah Supreme Court Standing Order No. 12
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Standing Order No. 12 governs expungement of appellate court records. The prerequisite is an existing district court order expunging the entire trial court record and the records held by other government entities. What is filed with the Utah Supreme Court, and served on the Utah Attorney General, is a written petition, a copy of the district court expungement petition, a certified copy of the district court expungement order, and a proposed redacted appellate opinion replacing the petitioner's name with initials or a pseudonym and redacting address, birthdate and government identification numbers. The Attorney General has 30 days from service to object to the expungement or to the proposed redaction. If granted, appellate records including briefs are sealed, the published opinion is replaced with the redacted version, and the appellate courts notify LexisNexis and Westlaw; other publishers are not legally required to redact. Utah Courts states expressly that there are no forms for this.

tracks.legalName: Cannabis possession conviction expungement petition, Utah Code 77-40a-305 and 77-40a-306(1)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Sections 77-40a-305 and 77-40a-306(1) allow a petition for a conviction related to cannabis possession without a certificate of eligibility, where the petition makes the required showing. The petitioner must show a qualifying condition at the time of the arrest or citation; that the cannabis was in a form allowed by law, meaning tablet, capsule, concentrated liquid or viscous oil, liquid suspension, topical, transdermal, sublingual, gelatinous cube or lozenge, resin or wax, or unprocessed flower in a compliant container, or a form measured in grams, milligrams or millilitres; and that the amount did not exceed the medicinal amount, up to 113 grams by weight of unprocessed cannabis in a medicinal dosage form, or 20 grams of total composite tetrahydrocannabinol in a cannabis product in medicinal dosage form. The citation question the controlling review left open is resolved: section 77-40a-305(4)(a), read at its official locator on 2026-08-06, itself cites Section 26B-4-201, which defines a qualifying condition by reference to Section 26B-4-203 where the conditions are listed. Title 26 Chapter 61a, which Utah Courts materials still cite, publishes no current version on the Legislature's site. The packet is cover sheet 1044XX, petition 1003EX, order 1023EX, and the 1146XX and 1148XX forms.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of a conviction on a certificate of eligibility, Utah Code 77-40a-303
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A conviction may be expunged on petition where all fines and interest are paid in full, all restitution is paid in full, and the applicable waiting period has elapsed, counted from the date the case finished, release from incarceration, or the end of probation or parole, whichever is most recent. The periods are ten years for a misdemeanour under 41-6a-501(2) and a felony under 58-37-8(2)(g); seven years for a felony; five years for a class A misdemeanour and for felony drug possession; four years for a class B misdemeanour; and three years for any other misdemeanour or infraction. Capital felonies, first degree felonies, violent felonies under 76-3-203.5(1)(c)(i), felony automobile homicide, felony DUI under 41-6a-501(2), registerable sex offences under 77-41-102 and registerable child abuse offences under 77-43-102(2) are permanently ineligible. The conviction-count bars at 77-40a-303(4) and (5) are measured against the entire criminal history including previously expunged and out-of-state convictions, with a separate allowance of up to four drug possession offences and a mixed-episode counting rule at 77-40a-303(6). Relief is discretionary in the sense that the court must find by clear and convincing evidence that expungement is not contrary to the public interest, and the petition form itself asks the petitioner to explain why.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of a case dismissed with prejudice, Utah Code 77-40a-302(1)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A case dismissed with prejudice may be expunged on petition at least 30 days after the arrest, on a certificate of eligibility from BCI. The same disposition is separately eligible for automatic expungement 180 days after dismissal under 77-40a-206, so the petition is the faster paid route to the same result and the free route must be disclosed before payment. Where the case came through a plea in abeyance, the case must actually have been dismissed; in some courts a Motion to Dismiss must be filed first using the general motions forms, which is a prerequisite step outside the expungement packet.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of a case dismissed without prejudice, Utah Code 77-40a-302(1) and 77-40a-306(2)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A case dismissed without prejudice may be expunged on petition at least 30 days after the arrest, and either the prosecutor consents in writing to the expungement or at least 180 days have passed since the dismissal. Under 77-40a-306(2) a prosecutor opposing expungement of a case dismissed without prejudice, or without condition, must have a good faith basis for intending to refile, and the court must consider how often that basis has been asserted. If the court denies on that ground, the petitioner may apply again for a certificate if charges are not refiled within 180 days after the denial.

tracks.legalName: Expungement where the statute of limitations has expired, Utah Code 77-40a-302(1)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Expiry of the statute of limitations on all charges in the case is a qualifying event under 77-40a-302(1), and BCI lists failure to meet it as a denial reason under 77-40a-302(1)(b)(v). A certificate of eligibility is required, which means BCI applies the limitations screen at the certificate stage. That is a meaningful protection in product terms: LegalEase does not have to compute a limitations period to route this track, because BCI will refuse the certificate if the period has not run.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of an arrest where no charges were filed, Utah Code 77-40a-302(1)

tracks.legalName: Motion to remove the link between personal identifying information and a dismissed criminal case, Utah Code 77-40a-105
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06. An individual whose criminal case is dismissed may move the court for an order removing the link between the individual's personal identifying information and the dismissed case in any publicly searchable database of the Utah state courts. Personal identifying information means a current name, former name, nickname or alias, together with date of birth. The court shall grant the motion if 30 days have passed from the day the case was dismissed, no appeal was filed within that 30-day period, and no charge in the case was a domestic violence offence as defined in Section 77-36-1. Relief is ministerial rather than discretionary once those three conditions are met. Two express limits define what the remedy is worth: under subsection (3) removing the link does not affect a prosecuting, arresting or other agency's records, and under subsection (4) the case history, unless expunged under the chapter, remains public and accessible through a search by case number. The remedy therefore breaks the name-to-case search path in the state courts' public database and does nothing else. The companion provision at Utah Code 78B-7-1002.1 gives the same relief to a person against whom a civil protective order or civil stalking injunction was sought and denied; that branch is a civil matter outside the record-clearing product scope and is not built here.

tracks.legalName: Expungement on a special certificate, Utah Code 77-40a-304(1)(c) and Utah Admin. Code R722-350-4(4)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where BCI cannot obtain disposition information for a criminal episode, or cannot determine whether the petitioner meets the requirements, after reasonable research, it offers a special certificate per criminal episode on payment of the issuance fee. The consequence is that the court rather than BCI makes the final eligibility determination and the evidentiary burden shifts to the petitioner at the hearing. Where the petitioner requested a fee waiver, BCI does not charge an issuance fee for the special certificate; if the court then finds the petitioner not indigent, the issuance fee must be paid before BCI will process the expungement order. The special certificate track uses a different petition and order from the certificate-of-eligibility track, which is why it is a distinct track rather than a variant.

tracks.legalName: Traffic conviction expungement petition, Utah Code 77-40a-305
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 77-40a-305 excuses the certificate of eligibility requirement for the traffic conviction petition, and BCI expressly directs traffic expungement enquiries to the court and states that no BCI application is needed. Eligible records are traffic offense convictions as defined at 77-40a-101 — infractions and class B or C misdemeanours under Title 41 Chapter 6a, Title 53 Chapter 3 Part 2 and Title 73 Chapter 18, plus substantially similar local ordinances — excluding driving under the influence and reckless driving under Title 41 Chapter 6a Part 5 and the boating equivalents. The track exists because a petition is faster than waiting five or six years for automatic deletion under 77-40a-202, at the cost of a filing fee. The packet is the civil cover sheet 1044XX, petition 1002EX, order 1022EX, and the 1146XX and 1148XX forms.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Sealing of Misdemeanour Non-Convictions for People With Otherwise Clean Records, Va. Code § 19.2-392.11
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 19.2-392.11 reaches misdemeanour offences resulting in acquittal, nolle prosequi or dismissal for a person with no convictions and no deferred and dismissed offences on their criminal history record. State Police identify finalised dispositions and provide an electronic list to the Office of the Executive Secretary and to circuit court clerks whose case management systems interface with State Police under § 17.1-502(B1), and the Executive Secretary provides lists to participating circuit court clerks on at least an annual basis. The mechanism matters to the participant because the annual cadence and the interface requirement together mean the same record may seal at different times in different courts, and there is no participant-facing status portal for this before the State Police verification portal is built.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Sealing of Offences Not Resulting in Conviction, Va. Code §§ 19.2-392.8 and 19.2-392.10
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Offences resulting in acquittal, nolle prosequi or dismissal are reached by the automatic-sealing machinery in §§ 19.2-392.8 and 19.2-392.10. This overlaps the expungement track: where automatic sealing reaches the record the person gets restricted access at no cost and with no filing, but sealing restricts rather than removes, and § 19.2-392.13 preserves the use of sealed records for firearm eligibility determinations and NICS, fingerprint comparison in AFIS, research by the Sentencing Commission, Crime Commission and JLARC, and access by law enforcement employees. Expungement under § 19.2-392.2 remains available and remains the stronger remedy for a participant who wants the record removed. The choice between them is a real one and the packet presents it honestly rather than steering.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Police and Court Records After an Absolute Pardon, Va. Code § 19.2-392.2(I)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 19.2-392.2(I) provides that, notwithstanding any other provision of the section, upon receiving a copy pursuant to § 2.2-402 of an absolute pardon for the commission of a crime that a person did not commit, the court shall enter an order requiring expungement of the police and court records relating to the charge and conviction, and that the order shall state that the expungement is ordered pursuant to that subsection. The trigger is the court's receipt of the pardon copy, not a petition, and the outcome is mandatory. Subsection K then routes the order to State Police, who validate the accuracy of the record but expressly not its eligibility. There is no waiting period, no fee, no fingerprint step and no manifest injustice showing on this subsection.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Police and Court Records After a Writ of Actual Innocence, Va. Code § 19.2-392.2(J)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 19.2-392.2(J) provides that upon receiving a copy of a writ vacating a conviction pursuant to § 19.2-327.5 or § 19.2-327.13, the court shall enter an order requiring expungement of the police and court records relating to the charge and conviction, and the order shall state that the expungement is ordered pursuant to that subsection. The trigger is the court's receipt of the writ. No petition, no application, no waiting period and no fee are prescribed, and nothing is left for the participant to submit. The two cited sections are the biological-evidence and non-biological-evidence writs of actual innocence, both of which are litigated in the Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court of Virginia by a petitioner who is represented by the time the writ issues.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal an Ancillary Matter Left Behind by Automatic Sealing, Va. Code § 19.2-392.12:1(B) and (J)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 19.2-392.12:1(B) lets a person whose conviction or offence was automatically sealed under § 19.2-392.7 or § 19.2-392.11, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986, or under § 19.2-392.6:1 regardless of offence date, petition to seal a specifically identified ancillary matter left behind — a probation or parole violation, a contempt, a failure to appear, or a bail appeal tied to the charge. tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal an Enumerated Offence After Seven Clean Years, Va. Code § 19.2-392.12:1(A)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A free-standing petition track, not a backstop. Section 19.2-392.12:1(A) reaches an exhaustive list of offence provisions — a violation of § 4.1-305; a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-96 or § 18.2-103; a violation of § 18.2-119, § 18.2-120 or § 18.2-134; a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-248.1; a violation of subsection A of § 18.2-265.3; or a violation of § 18.2-415 — whether the disposition was a conviction or a deferred and dismissed charge, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. The single test is seven years since the date of conviction or of dismissal of the deferred charge with no conviction in that period of any law requiring a report to the CCRE under § 19.2-390(A), or of any other state, the District of Columbia, the United States or any territory, excluding Title 46.2 traffic infractions. What is not required is the whole of what makes § 19.2-392.12 hard: no manifest injustice, no rehabilitation showing, no restitution criterion, no felony-history bars, and no lifetime cap, subsection E confirming both that there is no limit on the number of petitions and that grants here do not count against the two-petition cap in § 19.2-392.12. Subsection I makes the outcome mandatory on the two findings. Subsection D carries a same-date rule: the petition may not seek sealing where the charge, conviction or ancillary matter was finalised on the same date as a conviction

tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal a Class 5 or 6 Felony or an 18.2-95 Larceny Felony, Va. Code § 19.2-392.12
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Petition sealing under § 19.2-392.12 reaching a conviction of, or a deferred and dismissed charge for, a Class 5 or 6 felony, or a violation of § 18.2-95 or any other felony offence in which the defendant is deemed guilty of larceny and punished as provided in § 18.2-95, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. Ten years must have passed with no reportable conviction, and the clock runs from the latest of five events, not two: dismissal of the deferred charge, conviction, release from incarceration, a finding that the person violated a suspended sentence, probation or parole, or release from incarceration following such a finding. A probation violation therefore restarts the clock. Three felony-history bars apply: never convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or any other felony punishable by life; no Class 3 or 4 felony conviction within the past twenty years; and no other felony conviction within the past ten years from the date the petition was filed. Four further criteria the internal reference omits entirely: rehabilitation demonstrated where the records indicate the occurrence involved the use of or dependence upon alcohol, a narcotic drug or any other self-administered intoxicant; court-ordered restitution on any charge, conviction or ancillary matter in the petition paid in full; not previously having obtained sealing of two other deferrals or convictions arising out

tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal a Misdemeanour Conviction or Deferred Dismissal, Va. Code § 19.2-392.12
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Petition sealing under § 19.2-392.12 reaching a conviction of, or a charge deferred and dismissed for, a misdemeanor, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. Seven years must have passed with no reportable conviction, and the clock runs from the latest of five events, not two: dismissal of the deferred charge, conviction, release from incarceration, a finding that the person violated a suspended sentence, probation or parole, or release from incarceration following such a finding. A probation violation therefore restarts the clock. Three felony-history bars apply: never convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or any other felony punishable by life; no Class 3 or 4 felony conviction within the past twenty years; and no other felony conviction within the past ten years from the date the petition was filed. tracks.legalName: Sealing of criminal history records of a person 18 to 21 years of age, 13 V.S.A. § 7609
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person who was 18 to 21 years of age at the time they committed a qualifying crime may petition the Criminal Division of the Superior Court for sealing 30 days after completing the terms and conditions of the sentence. Read at source on 2026-08-06: the section heading and the operative text both fix the band at 18 to 21, and § 7609 contains no reference to age 25 anywhere. The conditions are that restitution and surcharges ordered for any crime of which the person has been convicted are paid in full, subject to the § 7282 waiver, and that the respondent has failed to show that sealing would be contrary to the interests of justice. tracks.legalName: Sealing of a criminal history record where there was no conviction, 13 V.S.A. § 7603
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read in full at source on 2026-08-06. Section 7603 provides one remedy — sealing — reachable by three distinct routes, and Act 60 repealed subsections (c), (d), (e), (f) and (h), so no expungement route survives on a no-conviction record. Under (a)(1), unless either party objects in the interests of justice, the court shall issue a sealing order within 60 days after final disposition if the court did not make a probable cause determination at arraignment, the charge was dismissed before trial with or without prejudice, or the defendant was acquitted; nothing is filed and the duty runs to the court. Under (a)(2) the court may seal at any time if the prosecuting attorney and the defendant stipulate. Under (g) a person may petition at any time, and the court shall grant and issue the order if it finds that sealing serves the interests of justice or if the parties stipulate. Under (b), where a party objects the court schedules a hearing, and the defendant and the prosecuting attorney are the only parties. The burden on the (g) route is affirmative on the petitioner, unlike the § 7602 conviction tracks where the respondent must show the contrary.

tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06. On application of a person who has pleaded guilty to or been convicted of a crime under Vermont law committed prior to attaining 25 years of age, or on the motion of the court having jurisdiction, and after notice to all parties of record and hearing, the court shall order the sealing of all files and records related to the proceeding if it finds that two years have elapsed since the final discharge of the person; that the person has not been convicted of a listed crime as defined in 13 V.S.A. § 5301 or adjudicated delinquent for such an offence for ten years prior to the application or motion, and no new proceeding is pending seeking such a conviction or adjudication; and that the person's rehabilitation has been attained to the satisfaction of the court. tracks.legalName: Motion to Vacate a Void Drug Possession Conviction and Refund Paid Legal Financial Obligations, State v. Blake
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Blake relief rests on the conviction being unconstitutionally void rather than on any waiting period or clean record. It covers convictions based on RCW 69.50.4013 or RCW 69.50.4014, their predecessor statutes, similar local ordinances, and certain inchoate offences, which the Blake order forms state are unconstitutionally void and must be vacated, with legal financial obligations and accrued interest paid pursuant to those convictions refunded. The relief available is vacation, refund of paid legal financial obligations, waiver of unpaid balances, and full or partial case vacatur, in superior, district and municipal courts alike. The refund is the part participants most often do not know about. Blake is not the same as the RCW 9.96.060(6) treatment route: Blake is about a void conviction and the treatment route is about treatment or programme participation, and the same person may qualify for both, so both questions are asked.

tracks.legalName: Application for a Certificate of Restoration of Opportunity, RCW 9.97.020
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06. A certificate of restoration of opportunity is a court-issued instrument that operates on the collateral consequences of a conviction rather than on the record itself, and RCW 9.94A.030(11) treats issued certificates as part of the criminal history a sentencing court sees, which confirms it is a recognised instrument rather than an informal document. Its operative effect is at RCW 9.97.020(1): no state, county or municipal department, board, officer or agency authorised to assess the qualifications of an applicant for a licence, certificate of authority, qualification to engage in a profession or business, or admission to a qualifying examination may disqualify a qualified applicant solely on the basis of criminal history where the applicant holds a certificate and meets all other statutory and regulatory requirements, except as required by federal law or as exempted. The exemptions are extensive and must be encoded: criminal justice agencies as defined in RCW 10.97.030 and the Washington State Bar Association are exempt outright, and the section does not apply to the licensing, certification or qualification of accountants, bail bond agents, escrow agents, nursing home administrators, nursing, physicians and physician assistants, private investigators, receivers, teachers, notaries public, real estate brokers and salespersons, security guards, and

tracks.legalName: Request to Delete Non-Conviction Criminal History Record Information, RCW 10.97.060
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: The only real deletion mechanism in Washington, and it does not touch convictions. Non-conviction criminal history record information is subject to deletion from generally searched criminal justice agency files where two years or more have passed since a favourable disposition, or three years from arrest, citation or warrant for an offence where no conviction was obtained. The request goes to the Washington State Patrol rather than to a court: it is an agency request, not a petition. Two bars apply outright, the person being a fugitive and the case remaining under active prosecution. Beyond those the agency retains discretion to refuse on three common grounds: the disposition was a deferred prosecution or similar diversion; the person has a prior felony or gross misdemeanour conviction; or the person has been arrested for or charged with another crime during the intervening period. WashingtonLawHelp states directly that it is hard for information to qualify as non-conviction data under the rules, which makes deletion hard to obtain, and that expectation must be set before anyone pays. Where deletion is refused there is a fallback: RCW 10.97.040 requires agencies to check with the WSP for the most current and complete information before reporting a conviction, and RCW 10.97.110 supports a suit, potentially with attorney fees, against an agency that violates the requirement.

A person convicted of a misdemeanour cannabis offence who was twenty-one years of age or older at the time of the offence may apply, and if the applicant qualifies the court shall vacate. The covered offences are any offence under RCW 69.50.4014 from 1 July 2004 onward, its predecessor statutes including former RCW 69.50.401(e) from 21 March 1979 to 1 July 2004 and former RCW 69.50.401(d) from 21 May 1971 to 21 March 1979, and any offence under an equivalent municipal ordinance, with cannabis taking the RCW 69.50.101 meaning. No waiting period is stated. This is not Blake relief: Blake concerns a conviction that is void, and this route concerns a lawful conviction the legislature has decided to clear.

tracks.mechanismExcerpt: The domestic violence branch of the misdemeanour vacation statute, separate because it has a different waiting period, an added notice requirement, a count limitation, an affidavit trap and a different legal effect. The DV trigger does not require a RCW 10.99.020 designation: the court may determine, after reviewing the court file and the totality of the records including any prior RCW 10.99.020 convictions or comparable out-of-state or federal offences and the damage to person or property, that the offence involved domestic violence, so an agent screening only for a DV tag will misroute. tracks.legalName: Motion to Vacate a Felony Conviction, RCW 9.94A.640
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Felony vacation in the sentencing superior court. The applicant generally must first have been discharged under RCW 9.94A.637, and the certificate of discharge is a separate process and the most common blocker. Class A felonies are not available on this route. A class B felony requires at least ten years since the later of release from community custody, release from full and partial confinement, or the sentencing date, and no new crime in this state, another state or federal court in the ten years before the application. A class C felony requires five years on the same three-event latest-of test with a five-year clean period, except that a class C felony described in RCW 46.61.502(6) or 46.61.504(6) is carved out of that rule by subsection (2)(f) and then barred outright by subsection (2)(g). tracks.legalName: Petition to Vacate a Misdemeanour or Gross Misdemeanour Conviction, RCW 9.96.060(2)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Washington vacates; it does not expunge adult convictions. On a granted petition the court permits withdrawal of the guilty plea and entry of a not guilty plea, or sets aside the guilty verdict, then dismisses the charging document and vacates the judgment and sentence. The applicant must have completed all terms of sentence including satisfaction of financial obligations; at least three years must have passed since the later of release from supervision or probation, release from total and partial confinement as defined in RCW 9.94A.030, or the sentencing date; and there must be no new crime in this state, another state or federal or tribal court in the three years before the application. Since 2024 c 296 the three-year clock no longer restarts on the date legal financial obligations are paid off, and the court may be asked to cancel or reduce some of them. Relief is discretionary: the court may in its discretion vacate even where every requirement is met, which makes Washington unusual and means no outcome may be promised. On vacation the person is released from all penalties and disabilities, the conviction is not included in criminal history for later sentencing, and for all purposes including employment and housing the person may state they were never convicted.

tracks.legalName: Dismissal After Probation and Vacation of a Pre-1984 Conviction, RCW 9.95.240
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06, RCW 9.95.240 is one of only four routes RCW 9.94A.030(11)(b) recognises for removing a conviction from criminal history, and it has two distinct limbs. Subsection (1): every defendant who has fulfilled the conditions of probation for the entire period, or who was discharged from probation before the period ended, may at any time before the maximum period of punishment for the offence expires be permitted in the court's discretion to withdraw a guilty plea and enter a plea of not guilty, or, where convicted after a plea of not guilty, have the verdict set aside, and the court may then dismiss the information or indictment, after which the person is released from all penalties and disabilities resulting from the offence. The probationer is to be informed of this right in their probation papers. A proviso preserves the conviction for pleading and proof in any subsequent prosecution for any other offence, with the same effect as if probation had not been granted. Subsection (2)(a): after the period of probation has expired, the defendant may apply to the sentencing court for vacation of the record of conviction under RCW 9.94A.640, and the court may in its discretion clear the record if it finds the defendant has met the equivalent of the RCW 9.94A.640(2) tests as those tests would be applied to a person convicted of a crime committed before 1 July 198

tracks.legalName: Application to Vacate a Pre-1975 Treaty Indian Fishing Rights Conviction, RCW 9.96.060(4)
authority: United States v. Washington, 384 F. Supp. 312 (W.D. Wash. 1974)

tracks.legalName: Conditional Discharge for Possession or Attempted Possession as a First Offence (Wis. Stat. § 961.47)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where a person has not previously been convicted of any offense under Wis. Stat. ch. 961, or of any comparable federal, state or county ordinance offense relating to controlled substances, and pleads guilty to or is found guilty of possession or attempted possession under § 961.41(3g)(b), the court may, without entering a judgment of guilt and with the consent of the accused, defer further proceedings and place the person on probation on terms and conditions. On fulfillment of the terms and conditions the court shall discharge the person and dismiss the proceedings. Discharge and dismissal is without adjudication of guilt and is not a conviction for purposes of disqualifications or disabilities imposed by law upon conviction of a crime, including the § 961.48 second-or-subsequent-offense penalties. tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Where the sentencing court ordered at the time of sentencing that the record be expunged upon successful completion of the sentence, and the sentence included probation, jail or prison, relief is executed administratively. A person has successfully completed the sentence if the person has not been convicted of a subsequent offense and, if on probation, the probation has not been revoked and the probationer has satisfied the conditions of probation. Upon successful completion the detaining or probationary authority shall issue a certificate of discharge which shall be forwarded to the court of record and which shall have the effect of expunging the record. tracks.legalName: Participant Request that the Supervising or Detaining Authority Issue and Forward the Certificate of Discharge (Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(b))
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Section 973.015(1m)(b) makes issuance mandatory rather than discretionary: upon successful completion of the sentence the detaining or probationary authority SHALL issue a certificate of discharge, which shall be forwarded to the court of record and which shall have the effect of expunging the record. The triggering event is successful completion — no subsequent conviction and, where the person was on probation, no revocation and satisfied conditions. Where that mandatory certificate was not issued, or was issued but never forwarded to the clerk, the participant may write to the supervising or detaining authority asking that it be issued and forwarded. No statute or rule prescribes the contents of that request and Wisconsin publishes no official participant form for it, so the correspondence is drafted. The letter supports implementation of an expungement the court already ordered; it does not itself change legal status, and the certificate remains the authority's document.

tracks.legalName: Application to Expunge Records of Arrest, Trial and Conviction After a First-Offence Controlled Substance Conditional Discharge, W. Va. Code § 60A-4-407(b)

On fulfilment of the terms and conditions the court discharges the person and dismisses the proceedings without adjudication of guilt. tracks.legalName: Court-Ordered Dismissal and Expungement on Completion of the Test and Lock Program, W. Va. Code § 17C-5-2(j)(1)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 17C-5-2(j)(1) provides that any person under the age of 21 who drives with an alcohol concentration of two hundredths of one percent or more but less than eight hundredths of one percent, for a first offence under that subsection, is guilty of a misdemeanour; that a person charged with a first offence under the subsection may move for a continuance of the proceedings, from time to time, to allow participation in the test and lock program under § 17C-5A-3a; and that 'Upon successful completion of the program, the court shall dismiss the charge against the person and expunge the person's record as it relates to the alleged offense.' If the person fails to complete the program the court proceeds to adjudication, and a motion for a continuance may not be construed as an admission or used as evidence. The expungement is mandatory, court-ordered and automatic on completion: the subsection describes no petition, no application, no waiting period and no participant submission of any kind after the continuance motion. This closes the controlling review's build blocker asking which subsection of § 17C-5-2 carries the test and lock dismissal and expungement and which offences it covers: the answer is subsection (j)(1), and the population is first offenders under 21 with a blood alcohol concentration between 0.02 and 0.08 percent.

tracks.legalName: Civil Petition to Expunge Records of an Acquittal or Dismissal, W. Va. Code § 61-11-25(a)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Any person charged with a criminal offence under West Virginia law who has been found not guilty, or against whom charges have been dismissed and not in exchange for a guilty plea to another offence resulting in a conviction, may file a civil petition in the circuit court in which the charges were filed to expunge all records relating to the arrest, charge, or other matters arising out of the arrest or charge. Records reached expressly include arrest records, fingerprints, photographs, index references and other data in documentary or electronic form. The petition may not be filed sooner than 60 days after the order of acquittal or dismissal. There are no filing fees or costs. A hearing is discretionary; if the court sets one it must notify the prosecuting attorney and the arresting agency and give them an opportunity to respond. If the court finds no current charges or proceedings pending relating to the matter, it may grant the petition, seal the court records and order every other agency, including law enforcement, to expunge, each certifying completion within 60 days. Relief is discretionary in form. A person previously convicted of a felony may not file under this section at all.

tracks.legalName: Civil Petition to Expunge Records Following Completion of a Pretrial Diversion or Deferred Adjudication, W. Va. Code § 61-11-25(a) with §§ 61-11-22 and 61-11-22a
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Any person whose charges have been dismissed following full and successful completion of a pretrial diversion under § 61-11-22, or following full and successful completion of a deferred adjudication under § 61-11-22a, may file a civil petition in the circuit court for expungement of all charges originally brought, provided the charges sought to be expunged arose from the same transaction or occurrence. Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 61-11-22 caps a diversion agreement at 24 months and excludes any person charged under § 17C-5-2, directing such a person instead to the § 17C-5-2b deferral; § 61-11-22a operates on an entered guilty plea whose acceptance the court defers, for up to three years on a felony and two years on a misdemeanour, and on compliance the defendant withdraws the plea and the matter is dismissed. Two provisos in § 61-11-25(a) bear directly on this route: no Division of Motor Vehicles record may be expunged by virtue of any order entered pursuant to § 17C-5-2b, and charges dismissed by way of full and successful completion of a deferred adjudication may not be expunged for violations of § 61-2-28(a), § 61-2-28(b), § 61-2-9(a), § 61-2-9a, § 61-2-9(b) or § 61-2-9(c) where the alleged victim is a family or household member as defined in § 48-27-204. tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge the Record of a Conviction After a Full and Unconditional Pardon, W. Va. Code § 5-1-16a
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 5-1-16a provides that any person who has received a full and unconditional pardon from the Governor may petition the circuit court in the county where the conviction was had to have the record of that conviction expunged. The petition is served on the prosecuting attorney of the county where the petition is filed, and the petitioner must publish notice of the time and place the petition will be made as a Class I legal advertisement under article 3, chapter 59, with the publication area being the county where the petition is filed. On verification of the act of pardon and after a hearing to determine that good cause exists, the circuit court may enter an order directing that all public record of the conviction be expunged. A record expunged under the section may not be considered in an application to any educational institution in this state or in an application for any licensure required by any professional organisation in this state. Eligibility opens one year after the pardon and, separately, five years after discharge of the sentence for the pardoned conviction; both must be satisfied. First degree murder, treason, kidnapping and any felony defined in article 8B are excluded. tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Records of Conviction of Certain Felonies (Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1502)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person convicted of a felony, or of felonies subject to expungement under the section arising out of the same occurrence or related course of events, may petition the convicting court to expunge the records of conviction. At least ten years must have passed since expiration of the terms of sentence including probation; any court-ordered program must be complete and court-ordered restitution paid in full; the petitioner must have no other felony plea, nolo plea or conviction; the offense must not have involved the use or attempted use of a firearm except certain Title 23 offenses; and the offense must not appear on the statutory exclusion list. The court must find eligibility and that the petitioner is not a substantial danger to himself, any identifiable victim or society. One expungement under this section is permitted in a lifetime. Under subsection (m) the expungement restores any rights removed as a result of the conviction.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Records of Conviction of Certain Misdemeanors (Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1501)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: A person who has pled guilty or nolo contendere to, or been convicted of, a misdemeanor may petition the convicting court to expunge the records of conviction. The waiting period is at least five years for non-status offenses and at least one year for status offenses as defined by § 7-1-107(b)(iii), measured from expiration of the terms of sentence including probation and any court-ordered program. The offense must not have involved the use or attempted use of a firearm; a health care provider convicted of a § 6-2-313 offense against a patient in their care is ineligible. The court must find the petitioner is not a substantial danger to himself, any identifiable victim or society. One expungement under this section is permitted in a lifetime. Per the Wyoming Judicial Branch, the section includes cases of deferred adjudication and cases where the charge was later dismissed.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Records of Arrest, Dismissal of Charges or Disposition (Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1401)
tracks.mechanismExcerpt: On a verified petition to the court in which the proceeding occurred or would have occurred, the court may expunge records of an arrest, a charge that was dismissed, or a disposition where the person was not convicted, provided at least 180 days have passed, no formal charges are pending, and no disposition under § 7-13-301, § 35-7-1037 or former § 7-13-203 was entered to any charge arising from the incident, including to a different or lesser charge. Expungement classifies the record at the Division of Criminal Investigation so it is not disseminated except to criminal justice agencies for criminal justice purposes; the court file is sealed and a certified order is transmitted to DCI.
